## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{100}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can a safety check miss its deadline even when it runs on its own processor core?_

A correct refusal computed too late does not stop the motion it was meant to prevent. Separating a learned proposer from its permission path in software does not make the two independent while they still share memory, electrical power, clocks, or cooling. A burst of inference can then delay the check that should stop the machine, heat from the accelerator can slow the core that runs that check for seconds after the burst has ended, and a single supply or reset fault can silence both paths at once. None of these couplings appears on a software architecture diagram, and none shows up in average utilization, so a safety argument that has never been loaded on its real silicon rests on an untested premise. Moving the check to separate hardware removes some couplings and adds others, a communication delay and a longer chain of supplies and wiring, so no placement is independent by construction. Where each workload runs therefore decides whether the permission path can still refuse in time, and an action that crosses the causal boundary on a late refusal cannot be taken back.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Conduct a dependent-failure inventory of the caches, memory controllers, interconnects, supply rails, clocks, resets, and thermal paths that each candidate placement leaves shared between the proposal and permission paths
- Explain why average bus utilization cannot bound a deadline, and identify which contention mechanism (bandwidth queueing, bank conflicts, or shared-cache miss handling) threatens a declared worst-case execution time
- Evaluate whether shared power and reset paths can defeat a selected permission placement
- Analyze thermal coupling and clock throttling hysteresis between multi-tenant workloads across disparate physical timescales
- Size a windowed watchdog's service window from measured completion jitter for a non-blocking lock-free record exchange
- Select among static reservation, spatial partitioning, workload reduction, and physical silicon relocation from measured interference and timing allowances, and allocate the selected placement's dispatch-to-admission interval against the stopping budget
- Design an adversarial stress campaign whose falsification threshold is the permission path's declared worst-case execution time ($T_{\text{wcet}}$)
- Construct a placement record formalizing the deployment envelope that scopes loaded observed maxima, thermal headroom, bus arbitration, mitigations, and untested conditions for release review

:::

## The Silicon Substrate {#sec-placement-silicon-substrate}

When the warehouse mobile manipulator's permission check finishes late, its motor drives keep executing the last admitted command, and the loaded base covers distance that the stopping budget of @sec-enforcement never reserved. The control barrier filter, the stopping reservation, and the fallback ladder developed there hold only while the permission path completes its check inside its hard real-time deadline on every cycle. The enforcement record declares a worst-case execution time inside that deadline, a bound on the check running alone, and whether the bound survives while the learned proposers run beside it is a question about the silicon underneath. Workload placement decides which silicon executes each computation, and with that choice, which memories, interconnects, clocks, power supplies, and thermal paths each task shares with the others. In conventional computing, placement is an optimization over throughput, latency, or energy. On a machine whose refusals must arrive on time, it becomes a safety problem.

Modern silicon integration works directly against the separation the permission path needs. A contemporary heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) integrates general-purpose application cores, neural accelerators, real-time microcontrollers, and specialized safety islands onto a single monolithic die. On that die, these subsystems share memory controllers, dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) channels, system-level caches, on-chip network interconnects, voltage regulators, clock governors, and the physical package that carries away heat. While silicon integration lowers unit cost, board area, and inter-processor communication latency, it quietly couples through shared hardware the very execution paths that the software architecture keeps apart. The question placement must answer is whether the deterministic permission path can keep its deadline and its authority to refuse unsafe motion while the proposal path runs at full load on shared hardware. Answering it requires a bound on hardware interference for every shared physical resource, derived from worst-case timing analysis and validated under loaded stress tests.

On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the software architecture draws the proposal boundary between the Brain and the Nervous System as a clean logical boundary, and Part I adopted a working hypothesis about where that line falls in hardware, placing the permission path on a discrete safety microcontroller physically separate from the application SoC. The machine's two physical jobs show what that separation must guard against. For the mobile base, whose mass-dominated mobility spends stopping clearance, an interconnect stall during visual feature extraction on the proposal engine could delay the permission path's refusal while the loaded base approaches a rack end. Every tick of delay beyond the single cycle accounted for in the stopping budget is travel distance the machine never reserved. For the arm, whose contact-dominated manipulation spends force margin, a burst of neural accelerator traffic that evicts the permission path's lookup tables from a shared cache could delay contact force validation while the gripper presses against a spring-latched cage door. The monolithic SoC is therefore an architecture the machine must be able to reject on evidence, and the discrete microcontroller is a design claim that must survive a loaded test rather than be assumed.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The physical separation hypothesis for silicon partitioning is established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
:::

Assigning the permission filter to a dedicated processor core does not create an isolated failure domain. A core running in isolation may still stall on memory arbitration, slow down under dynamic clock throttling, or suffer transient voltage drops when adjacent accelerators become active. Memory protection units and operating system process boundaries enforce spatial partitioning by preventing unauthorized reads and writes across address spaces. However, memory protection hardware governs access permissions rather than access timing. The underlying interconnect crossbar, memory controllers, and DRAM banks determine when memory transactions actually complete. Establishing a sound safety case requires both spatial partitioning to prevent memory corruption and temporal partitioning to guarantee bounded service times for shared hardware resources [@kopetz2011real; @rushby1999partitioning].

::: {#dfn-placement-operational-independence .callout-definition title="Operational independence"}

***Operational independence***\index{Operational independence!definition} is the property that no activity, fault, or overload in the proposal domain can push the permission path's execution past its deadline or disable its authority to refuse, through any resource the two paths share.

1.  **Significance**: It is the premise under which the stopping budget charges exactly one permission tick of detection delay. Every tick that proposal-side load adds beyond that one is travel at speed $v$ that the irreversibility test $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ never reserved, and a stall of unbounded length leaves the test with no bound at all.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike spatial isolation, which private address spaces and separate cores supply, operational independence also covers time, supply, clock, reset, and heat. It is the placement-level form of what functional-safety standards call freedom from interference, the absence of cascading failures from one element into another of higher integrity [@iso26262].
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a separate core, or even a separate chip, is independent by construction. Each shared resource is a hypothesis that needs a bound, and a loaded test on the real silicon can refute it.

:::

Every placement claim must therefore explicitly identify the physical and architectural resources that could delay or disable enforcement, alongside the mechanisms that bound their mutual interference. A shared die and a discrete safety microcontroller represent competing design hypotheses regarding these hardware dependencies, not interchangeable processor selections. Evaluating either design begins with analyzing what each path must compute and the exact timing constraints governing its execution.

## Two Paths and the Resources They Share {#sec-placement-two-paths-one-die}

A mobile manipulator must verify kinematic clearance and collision margins on every tick while its neural proposal model computes the next trajectory chunk. The third law, proposal is not permission, already separates the two in authority; placement decides whether the hardware keeps them separate in time when the proposer is at peak load. The argument runs in three steps. It first sizes what each path computes on the design Part I chose, because each path's workload and timing allowance set how much interference it can absorb. It then inventories the physical resources that could couple the paths, and finally scores four candidate placements, the chosen one among them, against that inventory.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-machine-paths
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MACHINE PATHS: PROPOSAL AND PERMISSION BUDGETS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, @sec-placement-isolation-decisions,
# │          @sec-placement-hardware-allocation, @sec-placement-fallacies-pitfalls,
# │          @sec-placement-summary
# │
# │ Goal: Size the running machine's two paths from the registry before any
# │       contention: the chunk policy on the application processor and the
# │       enforcer tick on the discrete safety MCU.
# │ Show: 135 µs unloaded = 40 + 80 + 15 µs = 54,000 cycles at 400 MHz, against
# │       a declared 250 µs WCET and a chosen 400 µs deadline in the 1 ms tick.
# │       Ch4's response budget (@eq-nervous-response-budget) also charges
# │       50 µs of blocking and 40 µs of interference, so the tick's own
# │       execution, shared-hardware interference included, must fit
# │       400 - 90 = 310 µs, and the declared WCET leaves 60 µs for
# │       shared-hardware interference.
# │       The permission path's isolated rail holds up for 2 s (a selected
# │       premise recorded here; decided in Ch2, sized in Ch12). The 5 ms
# │       renewal-jitter allowance tolerates at most a 12.5 percent stretch of
# │       the 40 ms chunk inference (Ch8's HostContentionAllowance).
# │ How: Registry fields of the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle
# │      scenario; the three enforcer sub-costs are chapter-local.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import nanosecond, microsecond, millisecond, second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlacementMachine:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_inference = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, vision included)
    permission_rate = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen
    mcu_clock = RM.permission_mcu.compute.clock_rate  # category: illustrative (reference class)
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    unloaded = AISLE.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative
    wcet = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared, not measured)
    deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    rail_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)
    renewal_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-lease-sizing)
    sense = 40 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (encoders, IMU, evidence epoch)
    constraint = 80 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    write = 15 * microsecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (drive-frame staging)
    # Blocking B and interference I from the MCU's own lower- and higher-priority
    # work: the scenario bounds of Ch4's TickResponseBudget (notebook
    # nbk-nervous-response-margin), mirrored here because a chapter cannot import
    # another chapter's LEGO cell. Keep equal to Ch4; promotion to the aisle
    # scenario in MLSysIM is pending.
    blocking = AISLE.enforcer_blocking  # category: illustrative (Ch4 B, scenario bound; registry)
    interference = AISLE.enforcer_interference  # category: illustrative (Ch4 I, scenario bound; registry)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    chunk_slack = (chunk_period - chunk_inference).to(millisecond)
    unloaded_sum = (sense + constraint + write).to(microsecond)
    unloaded_slack = (deadline - unloaded).to(microsecond)
    wcet_margin = (deadline - wcet).to(microsecond)
    b_plus_i = (blocking + interference).to(microsecond)
    exec_ceiling = (deadline - b_plus_i).to(microsecond)  # t_enf ceiling under the full response budget
    shared_allowance = (exec_ceiling - wcet).to(microsecond)  # I_shared the declared WCET leaves before the deadline
    unloaded_cycles = (unloaded * mcu_clock).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    min_chunk_rate = (1 / lease).to(hertz)
    compute_after_sense = (constraint + write).to(microsecond)
    contention_stretch = (renewal_jitter / chunk_inference).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        abs((unloaded_sum - unloaded).to(microsecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Sense + constraint + write must equal the registry's 135 µs unloaded cycle."
    )
    check(abs(unloaded.to(microsecond).magnitude - 135.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: 135 µs unloaded.")
    check(abs(unloaded_cycles - 54_000) < 1e-6, "Canon: 135 µs = 54,000 cycles at 400 MHz.")
    check(wcet < deadline < tick, "Declared WCET inside the deadline, deadline inside the tick.")
    check(
        abs(wcet.to(microsecond).magnitude - 250.0) < 1e-9 and abs(deadline.to(microsecond).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9,
        "Canon: 250 µs WCET, 400 µs deadline.",
    )
    check(
        abs(blocking.to(microsecond).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9 and abs(interference.to(microsecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9,
        "Mirror of Ch4 TickResponseBudget: B = 50 µs, I = 40 µs.",
    )
    check(abs(exec_ceiling.magnitude - 310.0) < 1e-9 and abs(shared_allowance.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "400 - 90 = 310 µs; 310 - 250 = 60 µs.")
    check(wcet < exec_ceiling, "The declared WCET fits the full response budget.")
    check(abs(chunk_slack.to(millisecond).magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "The 40 ms chunk inference leaves 10 ms of the 50 ms period.")
    # margin_coupling_timescale_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 1 millisecond
    check(abs(tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: 1 ms permission tick.")
    check(
        chunk_period < lease, "Lease rule: the lease outlasts one chunk period, leaving the renewal-jitter allowance that absorbs the proposal link."
    )
    check(abs(rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Canon (D15): the permission rail holds up for 2.0 s.")
    check(chunk_period + renewal_jitter < lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus the 5 ms renewal-jitter allowance fits inside the lease.")
    check(
        abs(contention_stretch - 0.125) < 1e-9,
        "Matches Ch8 HostContentionAllowance: 5 ms of jitter is a 12.5 percent stretch of the 40 ms inference.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_inference_str = fmt_latency(chunk_inference, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_slack_str = fmt_latency(chunk_slack, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    permission_rate_str = fmt_frequency(permission_rate, precision=0)
    mcu_clock_str = fmt_frequency(mcu_clock, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    lease_str = fmt_latency(lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    min_chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(min_chunk_rate, precision=1)
    sense_str = fmt_latency(sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    constraint_str = fmt_latency(constraint, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    write_str = fmt_latency(write, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    compute_after_sense_str = fmt_latency(compute_after_sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    unloaded_str = fmt_latency(unloaded, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    unloaded_cycles_str = fmt_int(unloaded_cycles)
    unloaded_slack_str = fmt_latency(unloaded_slack, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_margin_str = fmt_latency(wcet_margin, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    blocking_str = fmt_latency(blocking, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    interference_str = fmt_latency(interference, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    b_plus_i_str = fmt_latency(b_plus_i, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    exec_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(exec_ceiling, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    shared_allowance_str = fmt_latency(shared_allowance, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    tick_ns_str = fmt_int(tick, unit=nanosecond)  # placement-record field nominal_period_ns
    deadline_ns_str = fmt_int(deadline, unit=nanosecond)  # placement-record field hard_deadline_ns
    self_watchdog_str = fmt_latency(self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rail_holdup_str = fmt_latency(rail_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
    renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    contention_stretch_pct_str = fmt_percent(contention_stretch, precision=1, style="prose")
```

### Proposal and permission execution profiles

The mobile manipulator partitions its control across two distinct execution paths with conflicting systems requirements. The proposal path runs the chunk policy on the application processor at `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_rate_str`, ingesting synchronized navigation and wrist camera streams to emit coordinated base velocity and arm joint targets. Its 99th-percentile (p99) inference latency, vision processing included, consumes `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_inference_str` (an illustrative benchmark; see the Reader Guide) of each `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk period. Operating entirely in unprivileged user space, the proposal path holds no direct hardware authority over the motor drives. In the design Part I chose, the permission path executes on a discrete safety microcontroller (MCU) at `{python} PlacementMachine.permission_rate_str`. On every tick, it validates the active trajectory and any candidate replacement against the stopping envelope derived in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes, staging admitted setpoints into the outbound EtherCAT frame destined for the drives. This routine must complete strictly within a chosen `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline inside its `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` tick. It executes within a privileged real-time domain on a dual-core lockstep controller,[^fn-lockstep-comparator-coverage] whose cycle-by-cycle comparator flags divergent execution. That hardware guard is needed because a software envelope check cannot diagnose a silent fault in the CPU core executing it. Only the permission path holds memory-mapped input-output (MMIO)\index{Memory-mapped I/O} access to the fieldbus master carrying drive commands.

::: {#dfn-placement-heterogeneous-silicon-partitioning .callout-definition title="Heterogeneous silicon partitioning"}

***Heterogeneous silicon partitioning***\index{Heterogeneous silicon partitioning!definition}\index{Silicon partitioning!definition} is the architectural allocation of stochastic, high-capacity cognitive workloads (perception, learned policy evaluation) and deterministic safety loops (safety invariant checks, admission and fallback) across specialized execution domains isolated in hardware.

1.  **Significance**: Placing high-capacity neural deliberation and real-time safety enforcement on the same general-purpose operating system or compute engine creates common-mode failures. Kernel thread preemption, dynamic memory allocation, and time-slicing between accelerator contexts add tail delay that no measured average bounds, and a permission path exposed to that tail can miss its physical control deadline.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike logical software process isolation (such as Linux containers or POSIX process priorities), silicon partitioning enforces isolation across independent hardware registers, tightly coupled memories (TCM), and dedicated peripheral buses.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming multicore CPU affinity provides true failure-domain separation, when the cores still share caches, memory controllers, clock trees, and power rails.

:::

These two processors execute distinct software stacks. Proposal inference, global scene-map updates, telemetry streaming, and fleet networking run on the application processor under Linux. While a real-time kernel patch reduces scheduler dispatch latency, it cannot bound latency tails introduced by unvetted device drivers, bus arbitration, or shared hardware memory controllers.[^fn-preemptrt-linux-latency] Similarly, zero-copy buffer designs reduce internal memory bus traffic, but they do not eliminate fundamental contention at the physical memory controller.

By contrast, enforcement and sensor validation execute on the discrete safety microcontroller as bare-metal firmware governed by a hardware memory protection unit (MPU),[^fn-mpu-iommu-isolation] with quadrature encoder counters, the inertial measurement unit (IMU) on its Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) bus, and hardware timer capture channels mapped directly to dedicated physical pins. Each candidate proposal arrives from the application processor across a board-level serial link and is published into local memory via the seqlock mailbox described in @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges. No dynamic random-access memory (DRAM)\index{DRAM}\index{Dynamic random-access memory|see{DRAM}} is shared across the two execution paths. The memory protection unit strictly isolates local state, while the dedicated peripheral bus completely insulates the enforcer's execution path from the host's memory traffic.

Admitting an entire plan is computationally distinct from executing the cyclic permission tick. For example, the whole-plan validation routine examined in @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff cannot execute as an uninterrupted task inside a 1 ms control loop without violating timing guarantees. Instead, the runtime scheduler must preserve the real-time tick either by executing admission as bounded, interruptible work or by moving it to a separate processor whose own timing is verified, and in either case admission ends with an atomic check of current state and sensor evidence immediately before activation. The running machine takes the first option. Whole-plan validation runs on the microcontroller as background work below the tick's priority, so the tick preempts it; the bounds that keep this background work from delaying the tick through the microcontroller's own buses and memory are listed in @sec-placement-dispatch-admission. The system resource ledger must account for the active trajectory buffer, the resident fallback plan, the temporary admission workspace, and worst-case interruption overheads. The proposal generation rate also does not set the interval between successful admissions. Qualification must show that the end-to-end pipeline (transfer, admission, and activation) preserves the lease renewal bound, a guarantee the tick deadline alone cannot provide.

Similarly, the full volumetric scene map remains anchored on the application processor. The permission path receives only a compact, bounded local evidence snapshot whose spatial coverage, state uncertainty, observation timestamp, expiration horizon, and cryptographic integrity have been pre-validated for the proposed motion and its associated fallback maneuver. Updating the host map, serializing the snapshot, transporting it across the bus, validating admission, storing it locally, and evaluating per-tick spatial queries all represent distinct computational costs that require separate accounting in the timing ledger. Under no circumstances may a synchronous query to the host processor stall the permission tick. If a proposed trajectory strays outside the validated bounds or lifetime of the local snapshot, the MCU must immediately reject it. Consequently, the microcontroller's static memory budget must prove that the local snapshot buffer and resident fallback trajectories fit comfortably alongside the compiled enforcement binary.

From an electrical perspective, the power delivery architecture isolates the microcontroller, low-voltage drive logic, and electromechanical spring-brake coils onto a dedicated safety rail. This rail incorporates a localized capacitive hold-up duration of `{python} PlacementMachine.rail_holdup_str` and carries zero load from the proposal subsystem. Hardware qualification must prove that severe voltage transients induced by motor acceleration or neural accelerator bursts on the shared battery pack cannot trigger an undervoltage reset on this isolated rail. This local energy reservoir sustains logic operation and holds the mechanical brakes disengaged throughout a controlled stopping sequence without supplying motive traction power. Achieving the powered deceleration profiles described in @sec-enforcement-four-rungs requires both an intact high-voltage drive path and an engineered sink for regenerative braking energy. If either prerequisite fails, the system must trigger a certified fail-safe fault response rather than relying on standard stopping-distance assumptions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The isolated permission rail and its hold-up sizing are established in @sec-body-permission-rail-isolation.
:::

On an unloaded machine, the initial computational budgets appear comfortably generous. Representative baseline costs on the safety microcontroller allocate `{python} PlacementMachine.sense_str` to sample motor encoders, read the IMU over SPI, and verify the proposal's evidence epoch; `{python} PlacementMachine.constraint_str` to evaluate kinematic and dynamic envelope constraints; and `{python} PlacementMachine.write_str` to stage admitted setpoints into the outbound drive frame. This yields an unloaded enforcer execution time of `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_str`, which corresponds to `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_cycles_str` cycles at the microcontroller's `{python} PlacementMachine.mcu_clock_str` clock frequency. Measured against the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` hard deadline, this baseline path yields `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_slack_str` of timing slack. Even the declared worst-case execution time (WCET) of `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_str`, the conservative design envelope established in @sec-enforcement-loop-budget, leaves `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_margin_str` of headroom.

However, this timing margin cannot be assigned entirely to shared hardware contention. The formal response bound of @eq-nervous-response-budget explicitly charges the tick for blocking $B_i$ by lower-priority tasks (`{python} PlacementMachine.blocking_str`) and interference $I_i$ from higher-priority tasks and interrupts (`{python} PlacementMachine.interference_str`), both arising from the microcontroller's own workload, as modeled in notebook \ref{nbk-nervous-response-margin}. Delay from hardware shared with the proposer is a different quantity: it lengthens the execution term $C_i$ itself. Consequently, a loaded tick satisfies its real-time deadline only if its raw execution time, combined with all shared-hardware interference, remains below the deadline minus these internal overheads (`{python} PlacementMachine.b_plus_i_str`), establishing an effective execution ceiling of `{python} PlacementMachine.exec_ceiling_str`. Under the declared WCET bound, shared hardware contention can introduce at most `{python} PlacementMachine.shared_allowance_str` of delay before the tick misses its deadline, and every placement analysis must charge this complete budget.

The declared bound, not the deadline, is the quantity a placement must defend. It bounds the tick's execution in isolation, and the chosen placement claims that proposal-side load adds nothing to it. A loaded tick that runs longer than `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_str` therefore refutes that claim even when it still finishes before the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline, because every margin downstream of the bound was computed on the premise it has just broken. Each coupling in this chapter is priced against that *falsification threshold*, which @sec-placement-testing-separation formalizes and turns into a test campaign.

On the application processor, meanwhile, the neural policy's `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_inference_str` inference latency leaves `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_slack_str` of margin within its `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_period_str` execution period. The enforcer's sub-costs above are a baseline model rather than an integrated measurement, and local spatial-query overheads must also fit within the cyclic allocation. Complete system qualification requires empirical measurement of the fully loaded control cycle, establishing precisely which spatial queries fall within constraint evaluation and accounting for any independent overheads; neither an unloaded benchmark nor an isolated query model can validate the declared WCET bound.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The spatial-query workload the safety microcontroller must answer each tick is established in @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps.
:::

### Shared microarchitectural failure domains and cyber-physical attack surfaces

Assigning tasks to distinct processor cores does not establish independent failure domains if the underlying microarchitectural silicon infrastructure is shared.[^fn-ac20193-multicore-interference] Beneath any software-level access control, four physical coupling mechanisms can bind the proposal and permission paths without appearing on an architecture diagram: memory subsystems, power rails, thermal dissipation paths, and clock distribution networks. Part I's design claims to sever each of them at the board level. The audit below takes the four in turn, states what each would do to a co-located permission path, and checks how the chosen board answers it.

Memory contention introduces the first, and often most severe, coupling. Operating system memory-map modifications trigger inter-processor interrupts that force Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) shootdowns across cores,[^fn-os-tlb-shootdown] while direct memory access (DMA) operations from high-throughput camera pipelines incur cache-coherence invalidation penalties.[^fn-hw-dma-coherence] More fundamentally, a time-critical control loop cannot read its sensor feedback buffers if an asynchronous accelerator client monopolizes the physical interconnect. In a Unified Memory Architecture (UMA), where neural network accelerators, general-purpose application cores, and real-time execution units arbitrate for a single pool of DRAM across a shared crossbar, a high-resolution vision pipeline or an aggressive DMA engine can saturate the bus and starve the permission routine of timely encoder and IMU feedback, however high its software thread priority is set. This mismatch between software priority and unmanaged interconnect contention is the **UMA crossbar trap**\index{Unified Memory Architecture!crossbar trap}, and @sec-placement-resource-contention prices the queueing delays and bank conflicts behind it. The chosen design avoids the trap by giving the safety controller exclusive ownership of its memory. Candidate proposals cross an isolated board-level serial bus into dedicated local SRAM, so no DRAM is shared between the two domains.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-board-rail
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED DRIVE BUS VS. THE ISOLATED PERMISSION RAIL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, the power-coupling paragraph
# │          (moved from the Nervous System chapter with its prose).
# │ Goal:    Name the bus the application processor shares with the drives and
# │          the converter lockout that resets the host when that bus sags.
# │ Show:    47.7 V nominal drive bus; the application processor's converter
# │          locks out at 33 V; a depleted pack starts 9 V above it.
# │ How:     Registry fields on RM (M6: 48 V drive bus, MiR250-class pack,
# │          MEAN WELL DDR-240C-24 converter); the sag screen is derived in
# │          @sec-body-power-integrity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_voltage, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlacementBoardRail:
    """The drive bus the host shares, and the lockout that resets the host."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom = RM.drive_bus_nominal  # category: datasheet (48 V-class pack, nominal)
    v_bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: datasheet (pack minimum)
    v_uvlo = RM.drive_bus_uvlo  # category: datasheet (converter input lockout)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_headroom_low = (v_bus_low - v_uvlo).to(volt)  # headroom a depleted pack starts with

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_bus_nom.to(volt).magnitude - 47.7) < 1e-9, f"Drive bus nominal drifted: {v_bus_nom}")
    check(abs(v_uvlo.to(volt).magnitude - 33.0) < 1e-9, f"Converter lockout drifted: {v_uvlo}")
    check(abs(v_headroom_low.magnitude - 9.0) < 1e-9, "Even a depleted pack starts 9 V above the converter lockout")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_bus_nom_str = fmt_voltage(v_bus_nom, unit=volt, precision=1)
    v_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(v_uvlo, unit=volt, precision=0)
```

Power delivery represents the second coupling vector. Although the host processor and the safety controller draw from a common battery, they do not share a power rail. The host application processor draws from the nominal `{python} PlacementBoardRail.v_bus_nom_str` motor drive bus through a dedicated DC-DC step-down converter that triggers an undervoltage lockout (UVLO) if the supply sags to `{python} PlacementBoardRail.v_uvlo_str`. While the steady-state margin analysis in @sec-body-power-integrity ensures that even a depleted battery pack remains above this threshold during simultaneous drive acceleration and peak neural inference, unmodeled transients or supply faults (a blown fuse, or a battery management system (BMS) contactor trip) can depress the bus and crash the application processor. Had the safety microcontroller shared this unisolated supply, that same brownout would reset the safety monitor simultaneously. Motor gate drivers incorporate internal hardware protections for such events: integrated undervoltage lockouts disable power MOSFET outputs when gate-drive rails collapse, and pull-down resistors prevent floating logic pins from triggering destructive shoot-through currents. Those protections keep the drives from doing harm, but a shared brownout would also extinguish the permission path, leaving the robot's kinetic energy unmanaged as it coasts with no controller to command a controlled deceleration. The dedicated, held-up rail removes this common-mode failure. While the host browns out and reboots, the safety microcontroller stays powered, detects the bus undervoltage interrupt, and executes a fallback stop.

Thermal dissipation and clock distribution introduce the third and fourth coupling channels. When co-located on a shared silicon die or bonded to a common heat spreader, heavy sustained compute workloads on the application processor raise junction temperatures toward thermal trip points. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) governors configured to protect the silicon package then throttle clock frequencies across the entire die, slowing real-time safety cores that share no code with the proposal pipeline. As demonstrated in @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling, thermal throttling introduces hysteresis that outlasts the transient compute burst that triggered it. Similarly, relying on a shared external crystal oscillator creates a fragile single point of failure: thermal drift, mechanical shock, or crystal fracturing desynchronizes both execution domains simultaneously. Utilizing a discrete microcontroller eliminates both vulnerabilities by providing a physically separated package, dedicated heat dissipation, and an independent quartz crystal oscillator.

Each coupling channel names a failure mode that would invalidate the separation, so qualification must test the isolation by injecting faults rather than by reviewing schematics. Four stress regimes evaluate the physical prototype, three aimed at the supply, clock, and link and one at the proposals themselves:

1. *Power-rail droop testing*: Injecting maximum-slew current transients into the drive bus to verify that the noise coupled onto the safety rail stays inside the microcontroller's specified supply tolerance, the limit the placement record's droop field carries.
2. *Clock glitching and frequency margining*: Verifying that the real-time core maintains deterministic instruction cycle counts under clock jitter and voltage fluctuation.
3. *Communication link flooding*: Saturating shared interconnects to confirm that safety-critical heartbeat frames and trajectory proposals retain their deterministic transmission windows.[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration]
4. *Numerical and semantic fault injection*: Streaming synthetic proposals populated with out-of-range floats, subnormal numbers, and IEEE 754 NaNs to verify single-cycle rejection without pipeline stalls or exception traps.

The comprehensive timing stress test designed in @sec-placement-testing-separation validates these boundaries against the declared WCET threshold.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The physical injection apparatus for supply, clock, and bus disturbances is operationalized in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

[^fn-os-tlb-shootdown]: **TLB Shootdown**\index{Translation lookaside buffer!shootdown}: When an operating system modifies page tables, it broadcasts inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) to invalidate stale Translation Lookaside Buffer entries across all active cores. Receiving cores must suspend thread execution and flush affected entries, introducing unbudgeted multi-microsecond stalls. In shared-silicon architectures, these unpredictable synchronization pauses destroy the cycle determinism demanded by inner motor regulation loops.

[^fn-hw-dma-coherence]: **DMA Cache Coherence**\index{Direct memory access!cache coherence}: Direct memory access transfers bypass CPU cache hierarchies, requiring explicit cache line invalidation or write-back operations to maintain memory consistency between peripherals and cores. Without hardware-enforced snoop filtering or explicit barriers, processors read stale sensor frames or overwrite pending actuator commands. These maintenance operations inject variable latency penalties into high-rate control routines unless static, unbuffered SRAM regions are dedicated to peripheral transfers.

[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration]: **CAN Arbitration**\index{CAN arbitration}: Controller Area Network protocols resolve bus contention at the physical layer using wired-AND dominant ('0') and recessive ('1') signaling. If a defective transceiver continuously asserts a dominant state (a "babbling idiot" fault), it monopolizes the shared physical bus and blocks all higher-level communication. Hardware bus guardians and dominant-timeout clamp circuits monitor transmission duration, physically disconnecting jabbering nodes to preserve network availability for remaining safety participants.

Any safety-critical design must still evaluate the alternative it rejects, a single shared die carrying both paths. On one die the four couplings collapse into one semiconductor package, and real-time cores that execute their instructions independently of the application cores remain coupled through each of them:

- *Memory:* Bursts of camera DMA, neural accelerator memory access, and high-volume diagnostic logging can stall the real-time cores' cache fills and delay their interrupt handling unless hardware arbiters enforce deterministic bandwidth caps.
- *Power and reset:* Steep di/dt current steps can droop a shared core rail, and a software-initiated host reset can take down a common reset chain, unless power and supervisor domains are strictly isolated.
- *Thermal path:* Heat from the neural processing units raises the substrate temperature under the real-time cores, which share the package's only route to the chassis.
- *Clock:* A unified on-die governor throttles the real-time cores' clock together with the accelerator's when that substrate temperature reaches its trip point, and a shared PLL or crystal carries any fault to both.

Beyond accidental contention, these shared silicon pathways expose a **cyber-physical attack vector**\index{Cyber-physical security!shared-die attack surface}\index{Hardware security!side channels and DoS}. An adversary who compromises the unprivileged proposal stack can generate malicious memory traffic or toggle accelerator power states rapidly. The traffic starves the permission routine of memory service, and coordinated current surges pull the shared supply down (@sec-placement-resource-contention prices both). An isolation claim must therefore hold against the worst contention the proposal domain can generate within its authorized hardware limits, and benchmarks of benign workloads cannot establish that bound.

Functional-safety engineering provides formal methodologies to analyze this shared inventory. On the mobile manipulator, the certified safety scope is deliberately circumscribed. The trajectory admission algorithms that validate learned proposals carry no formal safety integrity rating; the certified protective stop functions implemented in the motor drives and safety laser scanner bear that legal responsibility. The single rated safety function assigned to the microcontroller is the watchdog that revokes authority when the chunk lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent. It then commands a certified drive-level stop, safe stop 1 (SS1, a controlled deceleration followed by torque removal) or safe torque off (STO), whichever the risk assessment assigns to the machine's state. Keeping that rated function apart from unrated software components (the trajectory admission checks and the neural proposer) is a formal *safety decomposition*. Under international safety standards, such decomposition is legally valid only if the architect proves complete independence between elements, and workload placement directly determines whether this independence holds. Systematically identifying shared microarchitectural resources whose failure or overload could simultaneously compromise both paths is termed a **dependent failure analysis**\index{Dependent failure analysis!placement}\index{Common-cause failure!shared silicon}, mandated by ISO 26262 Part 9 [@iso26262] and treated as common-cause failure analysis under IEC 61508 [@iec61508]. The warehouse machine answers to industrial and mobile-robot safety standards rather than automotive ones (ISO 10218-2:2025, for instance, incorporates the collaborative-robot protections first defined in ISO/TS 15066 [@iso10218part2; @isots15066]), but the requirement of freedom from interference is the same in every domain. The resource audit of this chapter is that dependent-failure analysis carried out on physical silicon, with every coupling priced in the tick's timing budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The certified drive functions beneath the permission path, and the stop each failure triggers, are established in @sec-enforcement-certified-functions.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The industrial and mobile-robot standards that govern this machine, and where each one's evidence is generated, are developed in @sec-release-standards-map.
:::

[^fn-ac20193-multicore-interference]: **Multicore Interference Certification (FAA AC 20-193)**\index{Multicore interference!FAA AC 20-193 / CAST-32A}\index{Worst-case execution time!multicore certification}: Avionics met this problem first. The 2016 CAST-32A position paper named shared caches, interconnects, and memory controllers as interference channels, and FAA Advisory Circular AC 20-193, issued in 2024 and aligned with EASA's AMC 20-193, replaced it with formal acceptance criteria [@faa2024ac20193]. Its lesson for this machine is that a timing bound measured on one core is void on a multicore until every shared row of @tbl-13-placement-candidates has been analyzed or mitigated.

[^fn-preemptrt-linux-latency]: **PREEMPT_RT**\index{Preempt RT!kernel latency}: The Linux real-time patch set makes most kernel code preemptible and runs interrupt handlers as schedulable threads, and it was merged into the mainline kernel in Linux 6.12 in 2024 after about two decades out of tree [@kernelnewbies2024linux612]. It shortens the scheduler's latency tail but cannot bound delays that drivers, firmware, or shared memory add, so a PREEMPT_RT host needs a measured bound before it may carry any part of the permission tick.

[^fn-mpu-iommu-isolation]: **MPU and IOMMU**\index{Memory Protection Unit!spatial isolation}\index{IOMMU!DMA isolation}: A memory protection unit (MPU) checks each CPU access against a few fixed address regions without translating addresses, so its cost is constant and analyzable. An input-output memory management unit (IOMMU) applies the same check to direct memory access (DMA) from accelerators and camera interfaces. Both govern *where* a memory transaction may access without arbitrating *when* the interconnect serves it; they enforce spatial partitioning while delegating deadline guarantees to hardware bus arbiters.

[^fn-lockstep-comparator-coverage]: **Dual-Core Lockstep**\index{Lockstep processor!fault detection}: Dual-core lockstep runs identical instruction streams across two physical cores, typically offset by several cycles so that a single transient fault cannot corrupt both pipelines identically, while an integrated hardware comparator detects architectural divergence. While lockstep execution flags internal CPU faults, it offers no protection against algorithmically flawed envelopes computed from corrupted sensor inputs or common-mode voltage sags on shared power rails. Consequently, lockstep operation serves as one component of the safety microcontroller's overall watchdog architecture rather than a complete integrity solution.

### Four candidate placements against one shared-resource inventory

Because operating system process isolation cannot remove silicon-level couplings, hardware placement is the primary defense against common-mode failure. Four candidate placements for the permission loop span the options, from sharing everything to sharing only the battery, and each is scored row by row against the shared-resource inventory (@tbl-13-placement-candidates).

(a) *Shared application cores* expose the permission loop to operating system scheduling jitter, driver interrupt stalls, and kernel preemption tails, delays that can push execution past not only the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline but the entire `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` control period.

(b) *A real-time cluster in the host clock and power domain* dedicates execution cores to safety enforcement but shares the die's cache hierarchy, memory controller, core supply rail, clock governor, and thermal dissipation path. @Sec-placement-resource-contention prices its memory exposure, and @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling shows the clock throttling that rules this candidate out.

(c) *An on-die safety island* represents the architectural pattern implemented in modern automotive and industrial SoCs, offering far stronger isolation guarantees than candidate (b). For instance, the Functional Safety Island of NVIDIA's Orin-class SoCs integrates four dual-core lockstep Cortex-R52 processors, each equipped with private tightly coupled memory, surrounding 3 MB of on-island SRAM [@nvidia2023drivefsi]. The island executes from an independent crystal oscillator and a dedicated voltage rail, isolated behind hardware firewalls that block unauthorized access from the rest of the die. The application governor cannot throttle this clock, and an enforcement routine whose code and data reside in island memory never waits on host DRAM arbitration. However, several microarchitectural couplings persist: shared substrate temperature within the physical package, common reset and power sequencing logic, arbitration across the on-chip fabric carrying proposals or island DMA, and the common board-level power supply. Adopting an on-die island requires qualifying each shared row: reading back the configured firewall registers, tracing the power-sequencing logic, and running the loaded stress campaign of @sec-placement-testing-separation while the safety loop executes.

(d) *A discrete safety microcontroller* eliminates every on-die microarchitectural coupling, trading silicon integration for an explicit board-level transport link from the application processor, budgeted and characterized in @sec-placement-isolation-decisions.

Laid out on the machine's compute board, the four candidates differ in how many shared blocks stand between the permission tick and the proposer (@fig-13-placement-resource-map). Candidates (a) and (b) sit behind the application die's last-level cache, DRAM controller, clock governor, core rail, and fabric. The island (c) moves cores, crystal, and SRAM behind a firewall but stays in the same package and heat path. Only (d), a separate package clocked at `{python} PlacementMachine.mcu_clock_str` with local TCM and a `{python} PlacementMachine.rail_holdup_str` rail hold-up, leaves the die entirely and reaches it through a checked board link.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-resource-map-figure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VALUES DRAWN IN THE PLACEMENT RESOURCE MAP (FIGURE GUARD)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-13-placement-resource-map
# │
# │ Goal: Keep the hand-drawn labels of fig13_placement_resource_map.svg
# │       pinned to the registry.
# │ Show: MCU clock 400 MHz, permission tick 1 kHz, permission-rail hold-up 2 s.
# │ How: PlacementMachine fields; a failed check means the SVG label is stale.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import second, hertz, ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class PlacementResourceMapFigure:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    PM = PlacementMachine  # category: derived; calc-placement-machine-paths

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(PM.mcu_clock.to(ureg.megahertz).magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, "figure MCU clock label (400 MHz) is stale")
    check(abs(PM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, "figure tick-rate label (1 kHz) is stale")
    check(abs(PM.rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "figure isolated-rail hold-up label (2 s) is stale")
```

Tinted blocks are shared with the proposer on the application die (cache, memory controller and external DRAM, clock governor, core rail, reset chain, fabric, and the package's heat path), so a tick placed on the die can lose them to proposal-side load. The safety island carries its own crystal, rail, and memory but remains behind the shared fabric and in the shared package; the discrete controller, the machine's choice, reaches the die only through a checked board link and shares only the battery with it." fig-alt="Block diagram of the machine's compute board. On the right, a separate green discrete safety MCU package, badge d, with lockstep cores at 400 MHz and a 1 kHz tick, TCM, its own clock, a reset supervisor, and a local mailbox, receives a board link from the fabric, drives EtherCAT to the drives, and is fed by an isolated rail with 2 s hold-up. A battery and common board supply bar along the bottom feeds both sides."}

| Shared resource                        | \(a\) Shared cores | \(b\) RT cluster, host domain | \(c\) On-die safety island                   | \(d\) Discrete MCU                         |
|:---------------------------------------|:-------------------|:------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| **Cores and scheduler**                | Shared             | Separated                     | Separated                                    | Separated                                  |
| **Last-level cache and miss handling** | Shared             | Shared                        | Separated (private caches, TCM)              | Separated (TCM)                            |
| **DRAM controller and channels**       | Shared             | Shared                        | Separated if the tick stays in island memory | Separated                                  |
| **On-chip fabric carrying proposals**  | Shared             | Shared                        | Shared, behind a firewall                    | Replaced by a board link                   |
| **Core supply rail**                   | Shared             | Shared                        | Separated (dedicated rail)                   | Separated (isolated rail)                  |

: **Dependent-failure inventory of four placements**: Each row is a resource whose fault or overload could delay or disable both the proposer and the permission path. "Separated" means the placement removes the resource from the permission tick's path; it is still a claim that register readback and loaded tests must support. Only the discrete controller removes the die-level rows, and none of the four removes the common board supply. {#tbl-13-placement-candidates tbl-colwidths="[24,14,18,24,20]"}

On the inventory alone, candidate (c) is a strong contender. It separates the cache and miss handling, DRAM, core rail, and governed clock, the rows behind the strongest mechanisms the next two sections price, and leaves shared the die temperature, the fabric its proposals cross, the board supply, and a reset chain whose independence still needs evidence, each of which a qualification would have to cover. This verdict is provisional, since nothing has yet been priced, but the machine does not wait on it, because it adopts candidate (d) for a reason outside silicon capability. While the safety island exists on the physical SoC die, commercial edge modules packaging the application processor do not expose it to system integrators, reserving access for dedicated industrial platforms (@tbl-13-island-exposure). Because an unexposed, unprogrammable safety island cannot serve as a valid deployment target, safety enforcement must move off the primary module.

| Platform (vendor statement date)  | Safety island on the SoC                          | Available to the integrator | Source              |
|:----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------|
| **Jetson AGX Orin module (2023)** | Cortex-R52 island present                         | No                          | @nvidia2023orinfsi  |
| **IGX Orin platform (2023)**      | Same island                                       | Announced as offered        | @nvidia2023orinfsi  |
| **DRIVE AGX Orin (2023)**         | Island with dedicated crystal and rail, 3 MB SRAM | Yes, through DRIVE OS       | @nvidia2023drivefsi |
| **Jetson Thor module (2026)**     | Not supported                                     | No                          | @nvidia2026thorfsi  |
| **IGX Thor platform (2026)**      | Supported                                         | Yes                         | @nvidia2026thorfsi  |

: **Safety-island exposure on edge AI platforms, as of 2026**: The same silicon can carry an island that one product line exposes and another does not. Which island a placement can use is a property of the module and its software support, not of the SoC's block diagram, and a later edition should refresh this table. {#tbl-13-island-exposure tbl-colwidths="[30,28,20,22]"}

Commercial platform exposure is therefore itself an architectural constraint. A vendor block diagram illustrating isolated silicon domains establishes what the hardware could theoretically execute, but system developers can utilize only the execution resources unlocked by board support packages and platform firmware. While specific commercial product tiers change over time, the engineering requirement to audit software accessibility before committing to a workload placement remains permanent.

The third law (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}) says a proposal is not permission, and that separation is empty if the proposal can delay the permission decision through hardware the two share. The four candidates differ in which resources they force the paths to share, and even for the discrete microcontroller the separation remains a hypothesis about timing under load that only a measurement of the loaded tick can support.

Choosing (d) before pricing the shared die does not make the next two sections idle, for three reasons. Each mechanism they price turns the rejection of (a) and (b) from an assumption into evidence. Each also names an obligation the chosen design carries in miniature, because the microcontroller has its own DMA engines, interrupt controller, internal buses, and supply, and @sec-placement-dispatch-admission and @sec-placement-testing-separation return to them. And the same analysis is the qualification guide for an integrator whose module does expose an island. Unless a passage says otherwise, the numbers in @sec-placement-resource-contention and @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling describe the permission tick placed hypothetically on the application die, with the sub-costs and timing budget it has on the microcontroller. On a die, the first place proposal-side load reaches that tick is the memory system.

## Contention for Shared Resources {#sec-placement-resource-contention}

Had the mobile manipulator placed its permission path on the application SoC, camera DMA, neural weight fetches, telemetry writes, cache writebacks, and enforcement reads would compete for memory service. Their simultaneous bursts determine the queue seen by the enforcer. On the selected machine, those host-side bursts delay the observation and chunk rather than the permission tick. The permission path encounters their effects as evidence age, refusing stale evidence and entering fallback if no admitted chunk renews the lease.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Camera DMA ingestion and its contention for the shared memory bus are established in @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
:::

### DRAM bank conflicts, AXI4 burst slicing, and arbiter starvation

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-dram-timing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LPDDR5 ROW-CONFLICT PENALTY ON THE APPLICATION SOC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-resource-contention, @sec-placement-testing-separation
# │
# │ Goal: Source the row-conflict penalty (t_RP + t_RCD) that the loaded-read
# │       notebook and the stress suite charge, instead of a hand-typed DDR4-era
# │       14 ns.
# │ Show: at LPDDR5-6400 the command clock is 800 MHz (1.25 ns); t_RCD and the
# │       per-bank t_RP are 15 cycles each, 18.75 ns, so a conflict costs
# │       37.5 ns. 256 bits x 6400 MT/s = 204.8 GB/s, matching the registry's
# │       rounded 204 GB/s.
# │ How: Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400 (JESD209-5 timings as encoded in
# │      the Ramulator 2.0 preset: nRCD = 15, nRPpb = 15, tCK = 1250 ps); bus
# │      width and per-pin data rate from the brain SoC's registry memory
# │      (Jetson AGX Orin technical brief: 256-bit LPDDR5, 204.8 GB/s).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_, nanosecond
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlacementDramTiming:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lpddr5 = Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400  # category: datasheet (JESD209-5 via Ramulator 2.0 preset)
    pin_rate = RM.brain_soc.memory.pin_data_rate  # category: datasheet (registry; Orin technical brief)
    bus_width = RM.brain_soc.memory.bus_width  # category: datasheet (registry; Orin technical brief)
    bandwidth = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (registry, rounded)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ck = lpddr5.t_ck.to(nanosecond)
    t_rcd = lpddr5.t_rcd.to(nanosecond)
    t_rp = lpddr5.t_rp.to(nanosecond)
    n_rcd = (t_rcd / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    n_rp_pb = (t_rp / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_conflict = (t_rp + t_rcd).to(nanosecond)
    t_min = lpddr5.t_rcd_min.to(nanosecond)  # category: datasheet (JESD209-5 analog minimum, t_RCD = t_RPpb)
    n_min_cycles = math.ceil((t_min / t_ck).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    data_rate_mts = pin_rate.to("Mbit/s").magnitude  # one bit per transfer per pin
    bus_bandwidth = (bus_width * pin_rate / Q_("1 bit")).to("GB/s")

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(n_rcd - 15) < 1e-9 and abs(n_rp_pb - 15) < 1e-9, "t_RCD and t_RP are 15 command-clock cycles each.")
    check(abs(t_conflict.magnitude - 37.5) < 1e-9, "t_RP + t_RCD = 2 x 15 x 1.25 ns = 37.5 ns at LPDDR5-6400.")
    check(
        n_min_cycles == round(n_rcd) and abs(lpddr5.t_rp_min.to(nanosecond).magnitude - t_min.magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "The 18 ns minimum rounds up to the 15-cycle clocked timing, for t_RCD and t_RPpb alike.",
    )
    check(abs(bus_bandwidth.magnitude - 204.8) < 1e-9, "256 bits at 6400 MT/s is 204.8 GB/s.")
    check(abs((bus_bandwidth / bandwidth).to("dimensionless").magnitude - 1) < 0.005, "Bus arithmetic matches the registry's rounded 204 GB/s.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_rp_str = fmt(t_rp.magnitude, precision=2)
    t_min_str = fmt(t_min.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_ck_str = fmt(t_ck.magnitude, precision=2)
    n_rp_str = fmt_int(n_rp_pb)
    t_conflict_str = fmt(t_conflict.magnitude, precision=1)
    data_rate_str = fmt_int(data_rate_mts)
```

A small urgent read can wait behind a large transfer even when the memory bus is mostly idle over a longer interval. The deadline depends on the traffic already ahead of that read and on whether the controller lets it pass. This queueing delay, which arises when memory and DMA transactions share an interconnect and controller, is the mechanism inside the UMA crossbar trap\index{Crossbar bus and DRAM bank contention}, and its bound depends on transaction size, queue policy, and bank timing.

Each claimant's average demand follows from its transfer size and event rate. On a shared multi-channel LPDDR5 interface, camera DMA streams, weight fetches at the policy rate, the enforcer's reads, drive writes, cache writebacks, and logging together occupy a modest fraction of theoretical peak bandwidth on average. An engineer who inspects only that average concludes that most of the memory bus remains free. Memory crossbar arbiters and DRAM schedulers do not schedule average rates. They arbitrate discrete, bursty transactions, and two workloads with identical average throughput interfere with radically different latency profiles if one streams in small, sporadic packets while the other arrives in long, saturating blocks. The weight transfers that set the memory wall [@wulf1995] of @sec-brain-memory-wall are the long blocks here, and on a shared controller the proposer's throughput limit becomes the permission path's queue.

How long a safety read waits depends on transaction arbitration and DRAM scheduling. An accelerator moving weights in large $256\,\text{KiB}$ tiles generates discrete memory transactions across the internal system interconnect. The example assumes an arbiter that completes each granted burst before serving a different requester.[^fn-axi-burst-limits] Furthermore, while bus protocols provide quality-of-service (QoS) priority signals (`ARQOS`), commodity memory controllers frequently treat these tags as advisory unless strict hardware priority bypass with bounded preemption latency is explicitly certified in register configurations. Whether an in-flight transfer can delay the urgent read, and whether queued tensor transactions can pass it, depends on the selected interconnect and arbiter. AXI burst limits alone do not establish a service-time or starvation bound.

[^fn-axi-burst-limits]: **AXI4 (Advanced eXtensible Interface 4)**\index{Hardware!AXI4 burst limits}: Arm's AMBA on-chip bus protocol permits incrementing bursts of up to 256 beats and forbids any burst from crossing a 4,096-byte address boundary. At a 16-byte beat, one full burst is exactly one such page, which is why the notebook below splits a weight tile into one transaction per page. An urgent read that waits for the granted burst to finish, as this example assumes, is a property of the chosen arbiter, not an AXI guarantee.

Every memory request passes through four stages: the requester issues it, the interconnect arbiter grants it a slot, the memory controller queues it, and the target bank serves it. Each DRAM bank holds one open row in its **row buffer**. An LPDDR5 channel has 16 banks, divided into 4 bank groups at the higher data rates, or 8 larger banks, each formed by merging two, in an alternative mode [@steiner2022lpddr5]. A read to the open row (a *row hit*) needs only a column access. A read to a different row of the same bank (a *row conflict*) must first close the open row with a precharge ($t_{\text{RP}}$) and then open the new one with an activation ($t_{\text{RCD}}$). The memory standard sets a minimum time in nanoseconds for each step, `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_min_str` ns for both, and the controller can only wait whole cycles of its command clock. At the `{python} PlacementDramTiming.data_rate_str` MT/s data rate of the machine's application SoC, that clock ticks every `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_ck_str` ns, each step rounds up to `{python} PlacementDramTiming.n_rp_str` cycles, or `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_rp_str` ns, and a conflict adds `{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_conflict_str` ns [@luo2024ramulator]. Bank-group spacing, refresh, and bus turnaround add further terms, which @sec-appendix-systems-dram treats.

The controller also decides the order of service. Controllers that use **first-ready, first-come-first-served (FR-FCFS)**\index{FR-FCFS scheduling!definition} scheduling serve ready row hits before older requests that need a new row, which maximizes throughput [@rixner2000memory]. A streaming accelerator supplies an unbroken run of row hits across its weight matrices, so an FR-FCFS scheduler can keep passing the safety core's sporadic read until an internal starvation counter expires. Under a FIFO queue that lets no later arrival pass the safety read, the idealized wait is
$$t_{\text{queue}} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{Q}} \frac{D_{\text{vol},k}}{\text{BW}_{\text{peak}}} + N_{\text{conflict}} (t_{\text{RP}} + t_{\text{RCD}})$$ {#eq-placement-dram-queuing}
where $\mathcal{Q}$ holds the transactions ahead of the read, $D_{\text{vol},k}$ is each one's byte count, $N_{\text{conflict}}$ counts changes to a different row within an already active bank, and $\text{BW}_{\text{peak}}$ is an optimistic service rate. Arbitration overhead and refresh add to the result. Exceeding the sensing allowance first violates the allocation to that subtask; it does not by itself imply that the whole tick misses its deadline. The worked comparison below keeps the sense allocation, declared execution bound, and physical deadline separate.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-loaded-read
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PERMISSION PATH'S LOADED READ ON A SHARED DIE (REJECTED PLACEMENT)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-resource-contention, @sec-placement-fallacies-pitfalls
# │
# │ Goal: Charge a FIFO backlog on shared DRAM to the machine's 40 µs sense
# │       allowance and 400 µs deadline (less Ch4's 90 µs of blocking and
# │       interference, so 310 µs of execution), to show why the bound is a property of
# │       the memory controller rather than of the workload.
# │ Show: one backlog of 88 transactions (360,448 bytes) plus three 37.5 ns row
# │       conflicts waits 1.879 µs at the application SoC's 204 GB/s; a 4 KiB
# │       snapshot then reads in 1.899 µs, inside the 40 µs allowance, which
# │       absorbs 21 such backlogs; the declared 250 µs WCET is crossed after
# │       more than 82 backlogs (155 µs read), refuting the declared bound,
# │       while the deadline holds until more than 114 (215 µs read); priority
# │       bypass cuts the read to 0.04 µs. Confined to one of 16 channels, a
# │       backlog takes 28.4 µs: the allowance absorbs 1, the WCET 5. Bandwidth
# │       queueing alone is a weak threat under interleaving;
# │       @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms prices the strong one.
# │ How: calc_axi_fifo_contention with PlacementMachine's sub-costs; bandwidth is
# │      the brain SoC's registry peak (RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth), served
# │      at the full aggregate rate because addresses interleave across all
# │      channels; queue composition and snapshot size are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_, microsecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_axi_fifo_contention
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlacementLoadedRead:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sense = PlacementMachine.sense  # category: illustrative (sense allowance)
    compute_after_sense = PlacementMachine.compute_after_sense  # category: illustrative (80 + 15 µs)
    deadline = PlacementMachine.deadline  # category: chosen
    exec_ceiling = PlacementMachine.exec_ceiling  # category: derived (deadline less Ch4's blocking and interference)
    wcet = PlacementMachine.wcet  # category: chosen (declared WCET, the falsification threshold)
    tile_bytes = 256 * 1024  # category: illustrative (weight tile)
    camera_bytes = 64 * 1024  # category: illustrative
    telemetry_bytes = 32 * 1024  # category: illustrative
    snapshot_bytes = 4 * 1024  # category: illustrative (encoder, IMU, and evidence-epoch snapshot)
    transaction_bytes = 4 * 1024  # category: datasheet (AXI4 4 KiB boundary)
    # Premise: the controller interleaves physical addresses across all its
    # channels, so the backlog and the snapshot are both served at the SoC's
    # aggregate peak rate. A backlog confined to the snapshot's channel would wait
    # longer by the channel count.
    bandwidth = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (application SoC peak DRAM bandwidth)
    bank_switches = 3  # same-bank row conflicts; category: illustrative
    bank_switch_time = PlacementDramTiming.t_conflict  # category: datasheet (LPDDR5-6400 t_RP + t_RCD)
    channel_width = Hardware.Tech.Memory.LPDDR5_6400.channel_width.to("bit").magnitude  # category: datasheet (LPDDR5 x16 channel, registry)
    bus_width_bits = RM.brain_soc.memory.bus_width.to("bit").magnitude  # category: datasheet (registry)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    result = calc_axi_fifo_contention(
        tile_bytes=tile_bytes,
        camera_bytes=camera_bytes,
        telemetry_bytes=telemetry_bytes,
        safety_read_bytes=snapshot_bytes,
        transaction_bytes=transaction_bytes,
        bandwidth=bandwidth,
        bank_switches=bank_switches,
        bank_switch_time=bank_switch_time,
        compute_time=compute_after_sense,
    )
    backlog_bytes = tile_bytes + camera_bytes + telemetry_bytes
    queue = result["queue_fifo"].to(microsecond)
    own_read = result["own_read"].to(microsecond)
    loaded_read = (queue + own_read).to(microsecond)
    sense_left = (sense - loaded_read).to(microsecond)
    read_ceiling = (exec_ceiling - compute_after_sense).to(microsecond)
    wcet_read_ceiling = (wcet - compute_after_sense).to(microsecond)
    backlogs_wcet = math.floor(((wcet_read_ceiling - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_sense = math.floor(((sense - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_deadline = math.floor(((read_ceiling - own_read) / queue).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    bypass_read = (result["queue_priority_bypass"] + own_read).to(microsecond)
    # Contrast case: the backlog and the snapshot confined to one channel.
    n_channels = int(round(bus_width_bits / channel_width))
    result_1ch = calc_axi_fifo_contention(
        tile_bytes=tile_bytes,
        camera_bytes=camera_bytes,
        telemetry_bytes=telemetry_bytes,
        safety_read_bytes=snapshot_bytes,
        transaction_bytes=transaction_bytes,
        bandwidth=bandwidth / n_channels,
        bank_switches=bank_switches,
        bank_switch_time=bank_switch_time,
        compute_time=compute_after_sense,
    )
    queue_1ch = result_1ch["queue_fifo"].to(microsecond)
    own_read_1ch = result_1ch["own_read"].to(microsecond)
    backlogs_sense_1ch = math.floor(((sense - own_read_1ch) / queue_1ch).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    backlogs_wcet_1ch = math.floor(((wcet_read_ceiling - own_read_1ch) / queue_1ch).to("dimensionless").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(result["queued_transactions"] == 88 and result["tile_transactions"] == 64, "88 queued transactions, 64 of them from one tile.")
    check(abs(bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude - 204.0) < 1e-9, "The application SoC's registry bandwidth is 204 GB/s.")
    check(abs(queue.magnitude - 1.8794) < 5e-4, "360,448 bytes at 204 GB/s plus three 37.5 ns conflicts is 1.879 µs.")
    check(loaded_read < sense, "One backlog fits inside the sense allowance.")
    check(
        abs(read_ceiling.magnitude - 215.0) < 1e-9,
        "The deadline, less 90 µs of blocking and interference, leaves 215 µs for the read after 95 µs of compute.",
    )
    check(backlogs_sense == 21 and backlogs_deadline == 114, "The sense allowance absorbs 21 backlogs, the full-budget deadline 114.")
    check(abs(wcet_read_ceiling.magnitude - 155.0) < 1e-9 and backlogs_wcet == 82, "The declared WCET leaves 155 µs for the read, 82 backlogs.")
    check(bypass_read < own_read * 3, "Priority bypass leaves one in-flight transaction ahead of the read.")
    check(n_channels == 16, "A 256-bit interface of 16-bit LPDDR5 channels has 16 channels.")
    check(backlogs_sense_1ch == 1 and backlogs_wcet_1ch == 5, "Confined to one channel, the sense allowance absorbs 1 backlog and the WCET 5.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    sense_str = fmt_latency(sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    sense_us_str = fmt(sense.to(microsecond).magnitude, precision=0)
    compute_after_sense_str = fmt_latency(compute_after_sense, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    b_plus_i_str = PlacementMachine.b_plus_i_str
    exec_ceiling_str = PlacementMachine.exec_ceiling_str
    n_tx_str = fmt_int(result["queued_transactions"])
    tile_tx_str = fmt_int(result["tile_transactions"])
    backlog_bytes_str = fmt_int(backlog_bytes)
    snapshot_bytes_str = fmt_int(snapshot_bytes)
    queue_str = fmt(queue.magnitude, precision=3)
    own_read_str = fmt(own_read.magnitude, precision=3)
    loaded_read_str = fmt(loaded_read.magnitude, precision=3)
    sense_left_str = fmt(sense_left.magnitude, precision=2)
    read_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(read_ceiling, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    backlogs_deadline_str = fmt_int(backlogs_deadline)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    wcet_read_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(wcet_read_ceiling, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    backlogs_wcet_str = fmt_int(backlogs_wcet)
    bypass_read_str = fmt(bypass_read.magnitude, precision=2)
    bandwidth_str = fmt(bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude, precision=0)
    backlogs_sense_str = fmt_int(backlogs_sense)
    bank_switch_str = fmt(bank_switch_time.to("ns").magnitude, precision=1)
    bank_switches_str = fmt_int(bank_switches)
    n_channels_str = fmt_int(n_channels)
    queue_1ch_str = fmt(queue_1ch.magnitude, precision=1)
    backlogs_sense_1ch_str = fmt_int(backlogs_sense_1ch)
    backlogs_wcet_1ch_str = fmt_int(backlogs_wcet_1ch)
```

::: {#nbk-placement-loaded-read .callout-notebook title="The backlog budget"}
