Both the boundary contract and its accompanying hardware supervision remain non-negotiable across every workload placement strategy. Whether the machine learning policy and the real-time safety enforcer reside on distinct physical boards, separate heterogeneous chiplets, or partitioned cores on a single SoC, the architecture must coordinate an asynchronous data exchange and actively verify execution liveness. What distinguishes one placement from another is how much cross-domain interference the tick must endure, and every mechanism that isolates that interference has its own price in silicon area, bus bandwidth, and hardware complexity.

## Silicon Isolation Decisions {#sec-placement-isolation-decisions}

Suppose a loaded test catches one of these couplings, a tick that exceeds the declared bound under proposal load. The team then has four remedies, each paid for in a different currency: static reservation, spatial partitioning, workload reduction, and physical relocation to separate silicon (@tbl-13-replacement-decisions). The machine's own choice, relocation, is the last of them, and it carries a transport budget that the section closes by allocating. The table is a map of the remedies, and the mechanisms it names (bandwidth regulation, cache coloring, bank partitioning, and the rest) are developed in the paragraphs after it; its last column says when a remedy no longer suffices and the next must be considered.

| Remediation Strategy     | Target Coupling Layer                                            | Implementation Mechanism                                                                         | Systems Engineering Trade-Off                                                                    | Residual Vulnerability                                                                      | When to Escalate                                                                                     |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Static Reservation**   | CPU execution time, OS scheduling preemption                     | Fixed-priority scheduling, ARINC 653 time slots, per-core memory-bandwidth regulation (MemGuard) | Capacity withheld from other work, including during quiescent states                             | Micro-architectural contention beneath OS visibility (shared L3, DRAM bank conflicts)       | Memory bus or cache stalls violate real-time deadlines despite $100\%$ CPU core allocation           |
| **Spatial Partitioning** | Cache capacity thrashing, DRAM bus contention                    | Cache coloring or way partitioning, DRAM bank partitioning (PALLOC), Arm MPAM, MPU/IOMMU domains | Structural fragmentation; smaller perception working set may increase off-chip traffic           | Unpartitionable DRAM controller queues, row-buffer locality reordering, PDN voltage droop   | Measured rail disturbances violate characterized limits, or DRAM queue stalls exceed the bound       |
| **Workload Reduction**   | Memory throughput saturation, peak thermal power                 | Model quantization (INT8/FP8), context downsampling, halved policy rate                          | Degraded policy tracking fidelity; increased control phase lag near dynamic stability boundaries | Common clock distribution trees, shared Power Management Units (PMU), unified reset domains | Model accuracy drops below operational limits, or shared clock/reset faults propagate across domains |
| **Physical Relocation**  | Shared power, clock, reset, or unbounded controller interference | Separate enforcer MCU with independently assessed power, clock, memory, and sensor/actuator path | More board area and an external communication budget                                             | Harness, transceiver, and common-supply faults remain                                       | Choose when the shared die cannot provide evidence for required timing and fault containment         |

: **Workload re-placement and isolation decision matrix**: Remediation pathways for when a test falsifies independence on shared silicon. Each remedy trades distinct engineering currencies (throughput, capacity, latency, board footprint) to eliminate contention channels before escalating to physically segregated silicon. {#tbl-13-replacement-decisions tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

### The four remediation pathways for shared silicon contention

The specific coupling channel dictates the engineering remedy, which must then survive loaded testing. A queueing bottleneck requires an enforced bound on service time, a cache capacity conflict requires physical separation of working sets, and a power supply or clock glitch demands an isolated fault domain that survives electrical disturbances. Trimming proposal workload demand can recover valuable operating headroom, but only a bound on worst-case residual interference can support a safety claim.

Under **static reservation**\index{Static reservation},[^fn-time-partitioning-tdma] physical workload placement remains unchanged while the critical execution path receives dedicated CPU time slices or interconnect slots. Reserving CPU execution time alone fails to bound memory access latency; the system interconnect requires an independent service guarantee, such as periodic time-division multiple access (TDMA) slots with fixed transaction beat quotas. When hardware crossbars lack native slot arbitration, system software must intervene. **Memory-bandwidth regulation**\index{Memory bandwidth regulation!MemGuard} assigns each processor core an access budget per regulation epoch, monitors memory transactions via hardware performance counters, and throttles any aggressor core with an interrupt-driven stall once it exhausts its quota until the next regulation window begins [@yun2013memguard]. By capping the cumulative traffic an aggressor can queue ahead of a critical transaction, bandwidth regulation converts the unbounded queueing multiplier $r_{\text{slow}}$ described in @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms into a provably bounded quantity. Throttling reads alone is not enough; defending against writeback-buffer saturation requires charging both explicit reads and dirty-line writebacks against the aggressor's allocation [@bechtel2019denial]. The predictable execution model takes this separation further on the real-time core, decoupling each task into an initial memory acquisition phase that pulls its working set into private scratchpad memory, followed by an isolated compute phase that touches zero shared interconnect resources [@pellizzoni2011predictable]. This design mirrors the boundary contract established in @sec-placement-boundary-contract: execute one strictly bounded read, then perform purely local computation. The systems penalty is stranded capacity: memory throughput remains reserved for the safety path even when the enforcer is quiescent. Had the warehouse mobile manipulator kept its permission path on the SoC, reserving memory bus slots for sporadic $4\,\text{KiB}$ sensor reads would throttle policy weight streaming across the accelerator, even with the robot base stationary.

[^fn-time-partitioning-tdma]: **Time Partitioning (TDMA)**\index{Time partitioning!TDMA}\index{ARINC 653!time partitioning}: Time-division multiple access gives each requester a fixed recurring slot, so its worst wait is one schedule cycle whatever the others demand. Integrated modular avionics made the same idea the basis of processor sharing: the ARINC 653 interface schedules partitions in fixed windows of a repeating major frame, and the assurance argument for such partitioning treats spatial and temporal separation as distinct obligations [@rushby1999partitioning]. The price is capacity reserved even when its owner is idle, the cost this paragraph charges to the proposer.

When contention arises from competing working sets thrashing shared hierarchies, **spatial partitioning**\index{Spatial partitioning} isolates cache ways or physical memory channels. For example, splitting an 8 MB last-level cache into 6 MB for the proposal policy and 2 MB for enforcer permission tables prevents cross-domain cache-line evictions, although constraining the perception working set can increase external memory traffic. Operating systems can enforce this isolation without special hardware primitives through **cache coloring**\index{Cache coloring}: the OS page allocator reserves physical memory frames whose page-index bits map to mutually disjoint cache sets [@mancuso2013realtime]. Extending this address-bit coloring technique to the bits that address DRAM banks assigns each domain private memory banks, eliminating the inter-core row-buffer conflicts modeled in @eq-placement-dram-queuing [@yun2014palloc]. Arm's Memory System Resource Partitioning and Monitoring (MPAM) extension implements these controls in silicon, combining cache-portion allocation bitmaps across shared caches with memory-bandwidth throttling registers downstream of the last-level cache [@linux2026mpam]. However, spatial cache partitioning does not isolate the shared MSHRs or unified writeback queues (@sec-placement-interference-mechanisms). Consequently, spatial partitioning must operate in tandem with bandwidth regulation, and neither mechanism eliminates the unified DRAM controller queue. Assigning fully dedicated physical DRAM channels removes controller contention entirely, but permanently deprives the proposal accelerator of memory bandwidth.

A **static-partitioning hypervisor**\index{Hypervisor!static partitioning} integrates these mechanisms across a single SoC. It statically binds CPU cores, physical memory ranges, and memory-mapped peripherals to isolated guest partitions during boot, dispenses with a dynamic runtime scheduler, and applies cache coloring to partition boundaries, as demonstrated in microkernels such as Bao [@martins2020bao]. This architecture represents the standard deployment pattern for hosting a hard real-time safety enclave alongside a general-purpose Linux stack on a common die. The formal scheduling foundation underpinning the asymmetry between proposal overruns and enforcer guarantees is **mixed-criticality scheduling**\index{Mixed-criticality scheduling} [@vestal2007preemptive; @burns2017survey]. In mixed-criticality theory, each task receives separate execution budgets calibrated to different assurance levels; when a low-criticality task overruns its baseline allocation, the runtime guarantees execution budgets exclusively for high-criticality tasks. On the running machine, the safety enforcer constitutes the high-criticality task, while the generative proposal model operates as the low-criticality workload. The lease protocol natively implements this degraded operational mode: a proposer that exceeds its inference deadline forfeits lease renewal without delaying or perturbing the enforcer's periodic permission tick.

When an application can tolerate degraded performance, **workload reduction**\index{Workload reduction} mitigates memory pressure and thermal dissipation through model quantization, reduced intermediate tensor transfers, pruned telemetry logging, or a decreased control policy update rate. However, this engineering relief comes at the expense of operational tracking fidelity. On the mobile manipulator, extending the action chunk period beyond the `{python} PlacementMachine.lease_str` lease allows safety leases to expire between renewals; maintaining continuous control authority requires successful chunk admissions strictly above `{python} PlacementMachine.min_chunk_rate_str`, even before accounting for renewal jitter. Steady-state producer throughput alone cannot verify this condition. Furthermore, post-training model quantization demands renewed experimental validation to ensure manipulation precision remains within tolerance. Finally, reducing average power consumption does not eliminate transient current spikes ($\Delta I$) or suppress inductive voltage droop ($L \cdot dI/dt$), which remain distinct electrical qualification obligations.

When on-chip software and architectural controls fail to bound shared-die interference, **physical relocation**\index{Physical relocation!silicon segregation} migrates the permission path to a dedicated microcontroller equipped with private SRAM, independent clock oscillators, a separate reset domain, and a galvanically or regulation-isolated power supply. Dedicated TCM eliminates DRAM bus contention entirely, while an isolated power rail supported by hold-up capacitance protects the safety monitor against host-side voltage collapse. Nevertheless, relocation does not eliminate verification overhead; it trades microarchitectural contention analysis for board-level signal integrity, transceiver qualification, and common-cause electrical fault containment.

Relocating the permission enforcer to separate silicon shifts engineering costs from on-chip microarchitectural arbitration to board-level interconnect latency and PCB layout complexity. The drive command bus delay ($T_{\text{bus}}$) remains identical because joint drives connect across an EtherCAT fieldbus regardless of compute placement. What physical relocation introduces is explicit proposal transport across an inter-chip link (a high-speed SPI link driven by DMA, an isolated PCIe Non-Transparent Bridge (NTB), or a differential serial bus) from the application processor to the safety microcontroller. While this board-level hop does not delay an enforcer cycle executing against existing, valid sensor evidence, it directly ages the observation state underpinning any newly admitted plan. This transmission time must therefore be charged against the dispatch-to-admission interval budgeted below. Furthermore, nondeterministic jitter in transport and admission consumes the `{python} PlacementMachine.renewal_jitter_str` renewal-jitter margin that the lease rule reserves between the `{python} PlacementMachine.chunk_period_str` chunk generation period and the `{python} PlacementMachine.lease_str` lease horizon. Host-side memory contention drains the same margin. An illustrative `{python} PlacementMachine.contention_stretch_pct_str` stretch of the inference exhausts the jitter allowance on its own, leaving zero margin for link delays or validation variance. Engineers must therefore evaluate lease renewal across measured end-to-end admission timestamps rather than inferring safety margins from upstream producer inference rates.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The renewal-jitter margin and lease renewal rule are established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing.
:::

Physical relocation also reshapes the sensor attachment topology. On the running machine, joint encoders and the IMU route directly to dedicated peripheral controllers on the safety microcontroller (hardware quadrature encoder counters and synchronous SPI channels), removing host-processor arbitration from the real-time feedback loop. Nevertheless, peripheral driver latency and register read jitter still require empirical qualification. In contrast, high-bandwidth perception sensors feed directly into the primary application processor: RGB cameras route over MIPI CSI-2 lanes, while lidar packets arrive over Ethernet. These heavy visual streams populate perception pipelines without traversing the microcontroller's constrained internal buses. Every silicon placement decision thus propagates across the physical hardware topology, trading on-die memory controller arbitration bottlenecks for board-level pin counts, differential trace routing, and serial link protocol overhead.

### The discrete placement's transport budget and the dispatch-to-admission interval {#sec-placement-dispatch-admission}

The budgets so far priced placements the machine rejected. The selected discrete placement has a timing budget of its own, and it closes the interval left unallocated in @sec-perception-latency-waterfall: the elapsed time from perception dispatching an observation frame to the safety enforcer admitting the resulting action chunk. This span is the **dispatch-to-admission interval**\index{Dispatch-to-admission interval!budget} $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, corresponding to the second phase in the system event ledger (@tbl-04-event-ledger). This interval encompasses the residual proposer inference pipeline following dispatch, serialization across the board-level interconnect, frame receipt and deserialization on the microcontroller, whole-plan kinematic validation, trajectory buffer activation, and the synchronization wait for the subsequent permission tick. Because the end-to-end stopping ledger originates at the initial sensor capture, every millisecond of $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ is base travel on aging evidence, and that travel must be paid for out of the stopping ledger's spare clearance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The composite stopping budget, which leaves the dispatch-to-admission interval out of the pre-brake delay and pays for it from the remaining clearance, is established in @sec-enforcement-composite-budget.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-transport-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DISCRETE PLACEMENT'S DISPATCH-TO-ADMISSION BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-isolation-decisions, @sec-placement-summary
# │          (Ch8, Ch12, and Ch14 name Delta_da; this cell allocates it)
# │
# │ Goal: Allocate Delta_da for the selected placement and compare it with the
# │       largest value the finished stopping budget can pay for.
# │ Show: SPI serialization of a 4 KiB chunk at 25 MHz = 1.31 ms; allocation
# │       40 (inference, conservative) + 1.31 (link) + 2 (deserialize) + 18
# │       (validate) + 1 (activate) + 1 (tick wait) = 63.31 ms; ceiling =
# │       spare / v = 131.01 mm / 1.3 m/s = 100.78 ms; reserve 37.47 ms =
# │       48.7 mm. Doubling the chunk or halving the link adds 1.31 ms; a
# │       second inference's worth of delay (103.31 ms) exhausts the spare.
# │ How: S-curve budget as in calc-placement-separation-budget; Delta_da is
# │      AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission (MLSysIM), which Ch14 imports too; its
# │      stages (inference, chunk size, link clock, and the deserialization,
# │      validation, and activation allowances of @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff)
# │      are loaded here only to display them.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import Q_, ureg, millisecond, millimeter, meter, second
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlacementTransport:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_bytes = int(AISLE.chunk_wire_bytes.to(ureg.byte).magnitude)  # category: illustrative (serialized chunk with header and evidence epoch)
    link_clock = AISLE.board_link_clock  # category: illustrative (SPI clock; one bit per clock)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (registry P99 incl. vision; conservative upper allocation after dispatch)
    t_deser = AISLE.t_chunk_deserialize  # category: illustrative (allowance of @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff)
    t_validate = AISLE.t_plan_validate  # category: illustrative (whole-plan validation allowance of @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff)
    t_activate = AISLE.t_plan_activate  # category: illustrative (activation allowance of @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff)
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (wait for the next permission tick)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit that sets the jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative + chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_link = AISLE.t_board_link.to(millisecond)
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(millisecond)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    budget = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_ceiling = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    reserve_t = (t_ceiling - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    reserve_d = (v_aisle * reserve_t).to(millimeter)
    travel_da = (v_aisle * delta_da).to(millimeter)
    delta_da_slow = (delta_da + t_infer).to(millisecond)
    t_replace = AISLE.t_capture_to_admission.to(millisecond)  # rows 1 + 2 of @tbl-04-event-ledger
    t_capture_onset = AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # rows 1 + 2 + 3

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_link.magnitude - 1.31072) < 1e-9, "4 KiB x 8 bits at 25 MHz is 1.31 ms.")
    check(abs(delta_da.magnitude - 63.31072) < 1e-6, "Allocation 40 + 1.31 + 2 + 18 + 1 + 1 = 63.31 ms.")
    check(
        abs((t_infer + t_link + t_deser + t_validate + t_activate + tick - delta_da).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "The displayed stages sum to the registry allocation.",
    )
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Canon: spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 100.77) < 0.01, "Spare / v = 100.8 ms, the budget's unallocated allowance.")
    check(delta_da < t_ceiling and delta_da_slow > t_ceiling, "The allocation fits; one more inference's worth of delay does not.")
    check(t_link < 0.05 * delta_da, "The link is a small share of the interval; inference and validation dominate.")
    # margin_dispatch_admission_budget_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 40, 1.31, 63.3 and 100.8 milliseconds
    check(abs(t_infer.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: 40 ms P99 chunk inference.")
    check(abs((AISLE.perception_age + delta_da - t_replace).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "L = t_age + Delta_da.")
    check(abs((tau_delay + delta_da - t_capture_onset).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Capture to onset = tau_delay + Delta_da.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_bytes_str = fmt_int(chunk_bytes)
    link_clock_str = fmt(link_clock.to(ureg.megahertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    t_link_str = fmt_latency(t_link, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_deser_str = fmt_latency(t_deser, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_validate_str = fmt_latency(t_validate, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_activate_str = fmt_latency(t_activate, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt(v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude, precision=1)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    reserve_t_str = fmt_latency(reserve_t, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    reserve_d_str = fmt_length(reserve_d, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    delta_da_slow_str = fmt_latency(delta_da_slow, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_replace_str = fmt_latency(t_replace, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_capture_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_capture_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-placement-transport-budget .callout-notebook title="The board-link toll"}

**Problem**: The machine's permission path runs on a discrete microcontroller that receives each chunk over a board link. How long may the interval from perception dispatch to admission last before the finished stopping budget has nothing left at the aisle speed?

**Variables**:

* Chunk policy p99 inference `{python} PlacementTransport.t_infer_str` (Illustrative), charged in full after dispatch, which is conservative because its vision stage already lies in the dispatch age of @sec-perception-latency-waterfall.
* Serialized chunk $D_{\text{vol,chunk}} =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.chunk_bytes_str` bytes on a $f_{\text{link}} =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.link_clock_str` MHz SPI link (Illustrative).
* Deserialization `{python} PlacementTransport.t_deser_str`, whole-plan validation `{python} PlacementTransport.t_validate_str`, and activation `{python} PlacementTransport.t_activate_str` (Illustrative allowances), and up to one `{python} PlacementTransport.tick_str` permission tick of waiting (Chosen).
* At $v =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.v_aisle_str` m/s the finished budget leaves $d_{\text{spare}} =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.spare_str` (Derived).

**Math**: Serialization takes $8\,D_{\text{vol,chunk}}/f_{\text{link}} =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_link_str`. The allocation totals $\Delta_{\text{da}} =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_infer_str` $+$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_link_str` $+$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_deser_str` $+$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_validate_str` $+$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_activate_str` $+$ `{python} PlacementTransport.tick_str` $=$ `{python} PlacementTransport.delta_da_str`, which the base covers as `{python} PlacementTransport.travel_da_str` of travel. The spare pays for at most $\Delta_{\text{da,max}} = d_{\text{spare}}/v =$ `{python} PlacementTransport.spare_str` $/$ `{python} PlacementTransport.v_aisle_str` m/s $=$ `{python} PlacementTransport.t_ceiling_str`, so the allocation leaves `{python} PlacementTransport.reserve_t_str`, or `{python} PlacementTransport.reserve_d_str` of positive reserve. Doubling the chunk or halving the link clock adds only another `{python} PlacementTransport.t_link_str`; adding one more inference's worth of delay, `{python} PlacementTransport.delta_da_slow_str` in all, exhausts the spare.

**Systems insight**: The board link that buys silicon separation costs about one millisecond, a small fraction of $\Delta_{\text{da}}$; proposer inference and whole-plan validation dominate the interval. Placement on discrete silicon therefore does not threaten the stopping budget, whereas a slower policy or a heavier validation kernel could exhaust it. The allocation is a target that qualification must confirm, not a relaxed runtime margin. The deterministic portion of $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ ages observation evidence and is charged here, while runtime variance between renewals drains the `{python} PlacementMachine.renewal_jitter_str` renewal-jitter budget, which host-side memory contention alone can saturate.

:::

With $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ formally allocated, the end-to-end event ledger (@tbl-04-event-ledger) contains no undefined timing windows. Total plan replacement latency from sensor capture to chunk admission (@eq-plan-replacement-latency) is `{python} PlacementTransport.t_replace_str`, while total elapsed time from capture to emergency brake onset in the event of an unresponsive proposer is `{python} PlacementTransport.t_capture_onset_str`. Both figures represent budget allocations that the loaded stress-testing campaign in @sec-placement-testing-separation must validate using physical hardware trace timestamps.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_dispatch_admission_budget_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal bars against a dashed ceiling line at 100.8 milliseconds: inference 40 milliseconds, board link 1.31 milliseconds as a thin sliver, and the dispatch-to-admission total 63.3 milliseconds."}

*The board link costs `{python} PlacementTransport.t_link_str` of a `{python} PlacementTransport.delta_da_str` budget.*
:::

Allocating the interval also exposes interference that the discrete placement keeps inside the microcontroller. The link's receive DMA engine and its completion interrupt, the fieldbus master dispatching motor drive frames, background whole-plan kinematic validation, and the periodic ingestion of evidence snapshots all contend for the microcontroller's internal crossbar, interrupt controller, and memory banks. Every potential interference path demands an enforceable bound: assigning SPI and fieldbus interrupt priorities strictly below the deterministic permission tick, allocating dedicated DMA channels, and mapping safety state to independent tightly coupled memory banks. The loaded validation campaign in @sec-placement-testing-separation must saturate the communication link and execute maximum-length plan validation while simultaneously triggering the refusal branch. Classical response-time analysis for the periodic tick, with its higher-priority preemption and lower-priority blocking terms, provides the formal static counterpart to those empirical stress tests.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Response-time analysis for a periodic tick, with its preemption and blocking terms, is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-timers.
:::

These remediation pathways determine which computing resources engineers must statically reserve or physically isolate. Two subsequent architectural decisions govern the remaining placement budget: whether any portion of proposal generation may be offloaded across an external network, and which candidate accelerator silicon completes autonomous missions within the chassis energy reserve. Off-board compute is first a timing question, and it comes first because energy efficiency matters only among architectures that already meet their deadlines.

### Off-board compute and mission energy

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-offload-admissibility
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OFF-BOARD INFERENCE AGAINST THE RENEWAL AND ADMISSION WINDOWS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-isolation-decisions
# │
# │ Goal: Apply the offload admissibility rule to a published remote
# │       vision-language-action deployment and to a published fog offload.
# │ Show: the renewal window is the 60 ms lease less the 5 ms jitter allowance,
# │       55 ms. RT-2's 5B model at about 5 Hz delivers one result every 200 ms
# │       (3.6x the renewal window); the 55B model at 1-3 Hz one every 333.3 ms
# │       at best. The paper reports rates, not latencies, so the admission
# │       ceiling is not compared. FogROS2 grasp planning, 14 s locally and
# │       1.2 s offloaded, lives on the task scale.
# │ How: lease and jitter from PlacementMachine; ceiling from
# │      PlacementTransport; remote rates and planning times are published
# │      measurements (Brohan et al. 2023, Sec. 3.3; Ichnowski et al. 2023).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond, second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

class PlacementOffload:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease = PlacementMachine.lease  # category: chosen
    renewal_jitter = PlacementMachine.renewal_jitter  # category: chosen
    t_ceiling = PlacementTransport.t_ceiling  # category: derived (spare / v)
    f_rt2_5b = 5 * hertz  # category: measured (Brohan et al. 2023, Sec. 3.3: 5B model "around 5 Hz", cloud TPU over the network)
    f_rt2_55b_max = 3 * hertz  # category: measured (Brohan et al. 2023, Sec. 3.3: 55B model 1-3 Hz; upper end)
    t_grasp_local = 14 * second  # category: measured (Ichnowski et al. 2023, abstract: grasp planning 14 s)
    t_grasp_fog = 1.2 * second  # category: measured (Ichnowski et al. 2023, abstract: 1.2 s with FogROS2)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    w_renew = (lease - renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)
    t_step_5b = (1 / f_rt2_5b).to(millisecond)
    t_step_55b = (1 / f_rt2_55b_max).to(millisecond)
    ratio_renew = (t_step_5b / w_renew).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(w_renew.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-9, "Renewal window: 60 ms lease less 5 ms jitter = 55 ms.")
    check(abs(t_step_5b.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-9, "5 Hz is 200 ms per step.")
    check(t_step_5b > w_renew, "The fastest published remote result interval exceeds the renewal window.")
    check(abs(ratio_renew - 200 / 55) < 1e-9, "3.6x the renewal window.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_str = fmt_latency(lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    w_renew_str = fmt_latency(w_renew, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_rt2_5b_str = fmt_frequency(f_rt2_5b, precision=0)
    t_step_5b_str = fmt_latency(t_step_5b, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_step_55b_str = fmt_latency(t_step_55b, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    ratio_renew_str = fmt(ratio_renew, precision=1)
    t_grasp_local_str = fmt_latency(t_grasp_local, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_grasp_fog_str = fmt_latency(t_grasp_fog, unit=second, precision=1)
```

Off-board computation operates under the exact same timing windows as a local board interconnect, but suffers from wide latency distributions across uncontrolled network infrastructure. An offloaded computational result is architecturally admissible if and only if the empirical tail latency of the network round-trip time combined with the tail processing latency fits entirely within the target admission window:
$$t_{\text{net}}^{\text{tail}} + t_{\text{proc}}^{\text{tail}} \le W,$$ {#eq-placement-offload-window}
where $W$ represents either the lease duration minus its renewal-jitter margin (`{python} PlacementOffload.w_renew_str` on the running machine) when the transaction renews dynamic authority, or the `{python} PlacementOffload.t_ceiling_str` dispatch-to-admission ceiling (notebook \ref{nbk-placement-transport-budget}) when admitting an entirely new action chunk.

Empirical robotics deployments demonstrate how severely this constraint restricts offloading. In RT-2, large vision-language-action (VLA) models ran in a multi-TPU data center queried over wireless networks; under real network conditions, the 55-billion-parameter model executed at only 1 to 3 Hz, while the 5-billion-parameter model reached approximately `{python} PlacementOffload.f_rt2_5b_str` [@brohan2023rt2]. At `{python} PlacementOffload.f_rt2_5b_str`, a fresh plan arrives only once every `{python} PlacementOffload.t_step_5b_str`, `{python} PlacementOffload.ratio_renew_str` times the renewal window, while the 55-billion-parameter model delivers outputs at best every `{python} PlacementOffload.t_step_55b_str`. Neither remote pipeline could sustain lease renewal on this machine. Because the published study documents overall throughput frequencies rather than an explicit breakdown between network latency and remote execution phases, one cannot determine whether a lower-latency wireless link could close the gap; qualifying any remote lease-renewal pipeline requires profiling the full tail distributions of both components. Instead, large remote foundation models are best positioned to synthesize coarse semantic goals or task decompositions, leaving high-frequency action chunk generation to an onboard policy. Coarser planning workloads operating on second-scale horizons represent prime candidates for edge offloading: for example, FogROS2 offloads ROS 2 compute graphs to cloud and fog instances, reducing grasp-planning latency from `{python} PlacementOffload.t_grasp_local_str` on local edge silicon to `{python} PlacementOffload.t_grasp_fog_str` [@ichnowski2023fogros2]. That acceleration speeds macro-task completion while leaving high-frequency microcontroller execution untouched. Packet loss or complete link disconnection must leave the onboard enforcer and its certified safe-stop routine fully operational. Neither remote offloading nor offline compilation eliminates the obligation to guarantee timely execution on local silicon.

Placement also decides which accelerator hosts the proposal path, and that choice reaches the permission path through energy as well as time. The chip's power is the load term that set the junction temperature in @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling, and it draws on the same battery whose sag the isolated rail must ride through. Among architectures that satisfy these timing bounds, candidate silicon must also complete the physical mission within the chassis energy reserve. Energy optimization often presents a subtle engineering trade-off: a lower-power edge accelerator draws fewer watts during active inference, yet if it extends execution latency, peripheral loads (lidar, depth cameras, cooling fans, and motor holding currents) remain energized longer. Conversely, a higher-throughput neural accelerator reduces mission energy only as long as faster compute actively shortens overall task duration. Once physical manipulator kinematics or vehicle velocity limits dominate the execution timeline, accelerating compute further merely burns excess power without saving task time, driving up total energy consumed per completed cycle.

For an assigned physical workload exhibiting steady-state compute power and baseline chassis power draw, total mission energy follows the relation:
$$E_{\text{mission}} = (P_{\text{chip}} + P_{\text{chassis\_static}}) \times T_{\text{mission}}$$
Evaluating this expression requires an empirical or rigorously modeled mission duration $T_{\text{mission}}$ for each candidate silicon configuration. Transient motor acceleration spikes, DC-DC converter losses, task retries, and quiescent dwell intervals demand explicit energy accounting whenever they diverge across platforms. Systems engineers cannot rank candidate SoCs simply by comparing datasheet figures such as peak tera-operations per second (TOPS) or nominal thermal design power (TDP). The workload to measure is the machine's own proposal pipeline, from camera ingestion through the chunk policy, and final silicon placement requires evaluating the compiled neural graph, its memory footprint, and the thermal assembly as one system. This chapter does not rank accelerators for the running machine, whose record carries no measured mission duration for any candidate; the relation states what such a ranking must measure.

The workload allocation model now accounts for explicit costs across reserved memory bandwidth, board-level transport latency, and battery energy draw. The engineering obligation that follows is experimental verification: generating reproducible empirical evidence that these isolation choices preserve permission tick deadlines and physical braking response under worst-case concurrent execution load.

## Empirical Verification of Silicon Isolation {#sec-placement-testing-separation}

The thermal hangover refuted candidate (b) from a model, but a placement that survives every model still has to face a measurement that could refute it. A claim of silicon isolation between an unverified learned workload and a safety enforcer must therefore reduce to a testable bound on enforcement latency and refusal availability. This bound must hold across all declared proposal workloads, junction temperatures, and operational modes. If shared-resource contention delays an enforcer refusal past its physical deadline, the claimed operational separation has failed, regardless of whatever architectural isolation was promised on paper.

```{python}
#| label: calc-placement-separation-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHAT A MISSED TICK COSTS THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-placement-testing-separation, @sec-placement-hardware-allocation
# │
# │ Goal: Tie the placement test to the machine's finished stopping budget and
# │       show that the bound, not the distance, is what placement protects.
# │ Show: WCET 250 µs < deadline 400 µs < tick 1 ms; budget 969.0 mm at 1.3 m/s
# │       with 131.0 mm before dispatch-to-admission travel; one missed tick 1.3 mm; renewal-to-onset 82 ms;
# │       an illustrative 10^7-tick trace that refutes the rejected placement.
# │ How: v tau + the jerk-limited S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance; jerk
# │      bound = the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit, as in
# │      @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix) + the aisle scenario's overheads;
# │      trace percentiles are illustrative.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond, millimeter, meter, second
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlacementSeparationBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    wcet = AISLE.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared)
    deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit, where the jerk bound is set)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative + chosen (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    n_ticks = 10_000_000  # scenario assumption; category: chosen (trace length)
    # Illustrative trace for the rejected placement (not a measurement)
    cold_p50 = 95 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    cold_p99 = 128 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    cold_max = 152 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    warm_p50 = 210 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    warm_p99 = 330 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    warm_p999 = 395 * microsecond  # category: illustrative
    warm_max = 468 * microsecond  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    budget = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    missed_tick = (v_aisle * tick).to(millimeter)
    deadline_share = (deadline / tick).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    renewal_to_onset = (t_lease + tick + t_bus + t_onset).to(millisecond)
    trace_s = (n_ticks * tick).to(second).magnitude
    trace_h = int(trace_s // 3600)
    trace_min = int((trace_s % 3600) // 60)
    trace_sec = int(round(trace_s % 60))

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(wcet < deadline < tick, "Declared WCET < deadline < tick.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak.")
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Canon: budget at 1.3 m/s is 968.99 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Canon: spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(missed_tick.magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Canon: one missed tick costs 1.3 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs(deadline_share - 0.4) < 1e-9, "The 400 µs deadline is 0.4 of the 1 ms tick.")
    check(abs(renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: renewal-to-onset bound is 82 ms.")
    check((trace_h, trace_min, trace_sec) == (2, 46, 40), "10^7 ticks at 1 ms span 2 h 46 min 40 s.")
    check(cold_max < wcet, "The cold trace stays under the declared WCET.")
    check(
        warm_p99 > wcet and warm_p99 + PlacementMachine.b_plus_i > deadline,
        "The loaded P99 breaks the declared WCET and, with Ch4's blocking and interference, the deadline.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    tick_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    budget_str = fmt_length(budget, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, precision=2)
    missed_tick_str = fmt_length(missed_tick, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    deadline_share_str = fmt(deadline_share, precision=1)
    renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    trace_s_str = fmt_latency(trace_s * second, unit=second, precision=0, commas=True)
    trace_h_str = fmt_int(trace_h)
    trace_min_str = fmt_int(trace_min)
    trace_sec_str = fmt_int(trace_sec)
    cold_p50_str = fmt_latency(cold_p50, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    cold_p99_str = fmt_latency(cold_p99, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    cold_max_str = fmt_latency(cold_max, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    warm_p50_str = fmt_latency(warm_p50, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    warm_p99_str = fmt_latency(warm_p99, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    warm_p999_str = fmt_latency(warm_p999, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    warm_max_str = fmt_latency(warm_max, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

### The worst-case execution time falsification threshold

The budget section of @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die introduced the permission tick's declared worst-case execution time ($T_{\text{wcet}}$) as the falsification threshold, and every mechanism since has been charged against it. This section states the threshold formally, because a test designed to refute a placement must name exactly which measured quantity it compares with that bound.

Worst-case execution time strictly bounds task execution in complete isolation. Microarchitectural interference from hardware shared with co-running workloads therefore does not appear as a separate term of the response-time bound (@eq-nervous-response-budget); it lengthens the execution term $C_i$, beside the blocking $B_i$ and interference $I_i$ that the microcontroller's own tasks contribute.

The pass-fail threshold for silicon isolation derives directly from the system specification. The machine's permission path specifies a declared worst-case execution time $T_{\text{wcet}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.wcet_str`, representing the isolated execution parameter $C_i$ in @eq-nervous-response-budget. It must complete each permission evaluation within a chosen enforcer deadline $T_{\text{deadline,enf}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.deadline_str`, which is nested inside the overall permission period $T_{\text{tick}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.tick_str`. When measured under operational load, total enforcer execution time is the sum of isolated execution latency and cross-workload hardware interference, as formalized in @eq-placement-falsification-threshold:
$$t_{\text{enf}} = t_{\text{iso}} + T_{\text{interf,shared}}, \qquad t_{\text{iso}} \le T_{\text{wcet}} < T_{\text{deadline,enf}} < T_{\text{tick}}$$ {#eq-placement-falsification-threshold}
where $t_{\text{iso}}$ represents the execution time of the permission path running with zero contention, and $T_{\text{interf,shared}}$ captures the cumulative delay inflicted by proposal-side activity competing for shared DRAM channels, caches, interconnects, clock trees, power distribution networks, and thermal budgets.

An ideal isolated placement claims that proposal-side execution introduces zero cross-workload interference ($T_{\text{interf,shared}} = 0$). Consequently, the declared bound $T_{\text{wcet}}$ serves as the **falsification threshold**\index{Falsification threshold!definition}. Because isolated execution cannot exceed $T_{\text{wcet}}$ by definition, any measured cycle under load that exceeds $T_{\text{wcet}}$ demonstrates that either the declared baseline WCET was underestimated or the shared hardware introduced an interference penalty that the architecture failed to eliminate. Either outcome refutes the timing contract of the placement. This holds even if the cycle completes before $T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$, because every downstream margin, from the deadline itself to the stopping distance budgeted for each tick, depends on that premise.

Conversely, observing a loaded execution cycle below $T_{\text{wcet}}$ does not establish that $T_{\text{interf,shared}}$ is zero. Empirical testing can decisively falsify a declared bound, but measurements alone cannot prove its universal validity. Any test campaign samples only the microarchitectural states it reaches, and microarchitectural timing anomalies can push the true worst-case latency beyond every observed cycle.[^fn-math-wcet-anomalies]

[^fn-math-wcet-anomalies]: **Microarchitectural Timing Anomalies**\index{Timing anomalies!worst-case execution time}\index{Worst-case execution time!timing anomalies}: A local speedup, such as an unexpected cache hit, can reorder subsequent pipeline or interconnect resource contention and paradoxically lengthen total execution time [@lundqvist1999timing]. Although first identified in dynamically scheduled out-of-order processors, timing anomalies also appear in pipelined in-order cores coupled to shared buses or caches [@wilhelm2008worst]. Consequently, composing local worst-case assumptions at each pipeline stage does not guarantee the global worst-case execution time, and empirical observation on an in-order core cannot substitute for formal timing analysis.

Even a small overrun invalidates the declared premise. It need not cause a collision on that tick, but it removes the guarantee beneath every downstream stopping and lease-renewal margin. Response-time verification charges the full bound from @eq-nervous-response-budget, $t_{\text{enf}} + B_i + I_i \le T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$, in which $T_{\text{interf,shared}}$ inflates the execution term $t_{\text{enf}}$, while $B_i$ and $I_i$ remain the blocking and interference from the safety microcontroller's own workload. Under the declared bound, shared platform hardware can introduce at most `{python} PlacementMachine.shared_allowance_str` of cross-workload delay before the enforcer violates its deadline, and every candidate in this chapter, chosen or rejected, is judged against that ledger.

Because a single permission tick at `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.v_aisle_str` corresponds to only $v\,T_{\text{tick}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.missed_tick_str` of vehicle displacement, engineers often underestimate the severity of a missed deadline. The physical stopping ledger, however, leaves little margin for error. Under the baseline assumptions compiled in @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget, bringing the vehicle to a controlled stop from `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.v_aisle_str` requires `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.budget_str`, which leaves `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.spare_str` of clearance within the `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance. That subtotal accounts only for the onboard stopping maneuver; it excludes the dispatch-to-admission latency $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, which is an allocated system budget rather than a measured property. Deducting the `{python} PlacementTransport.delta_da_str` allocated to $\Delta_{\text{da}}$ in notebook \ref{nbk-placement-transport-budget} shrinks the stopping reserve to `{python} PlacementTransport.reserve_d_str`. While the safety ledger can absorb the loss of an isolated $T_{\text{tick}}$, unmitigated microarchitectural contention does not produce predictable single-tick delays; it produces open-ended stalls that exhaust the stopping margin entirely. That asymmetry is why the thermal case of @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling disqualifies candidate (b) even though each of its late refusals slips only about one tick. The distance lost is small, but the placement has broken the bound on which every distance was computed, and a broken bound no longer limits how far the next stall can run.

Guaranteeing that the enforcer finishes before $T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$ also stabilizes the downstream feedback loop. When the system dispatches motor-drive command frames at a deterministic phase offset scheduled no earlier than $T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$, execution jitter never propagates to the actuators. Instead, the feedback controller encounters a constant computation delay equal to `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.deadline_share_str` of the tick period. Control engineers model this fixed latency directly as phase lag at the loop crossover frequency, mirroring the phase delay introduced by a zero-order hold.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The zero-order hold's phase lag, about half a sample period of delay, is developed in @sec-appendix-control-zoh.
:::

### Worst-case execution time analysis methods

A declared worst-case execution time is a formal timing commitment. Systems engineers substantiate that commitment through one of four established methodologies, each rooted in distinct operational premises [@puschner1989calculating; @wilhelm2008worst]:

*Static analysis* operates entirely without executing the binary on hardware. The analyzer reconstructs the control-flow graph directly from machine instructions, bounds every loop iteration, and applies abstract interpretation [@cousot1977abstract] to model the processor pipeline and cache states. This classifies memory references as definite hits, definite misses, or unresolvable states. The tool then solves an integer linear program [@li1995performance] to identify the longest feasible execution path: basic-block execution frequencies serve as decision variables constrained by structural flow conservation and loop bounds, while the objective function maximizes total cycle count based on block-level worst-case latencies. Static analysis yields a provably sound upper bound, provided the underlying microarchitectural model matches physical silicon. The prerequisite holds for the reference microcontroller, an in-order dual-core lockstep processor running out of tightly coupled memory without shared caches. However, static modeling collapses on commercial application multicores featuring out-of-order execution, undocumented interconnect arbitration, and non-blocking caches shared with arbitrary co-running tasks.

*Measurement-based analysis* executes the binary directly on target hardware under the most demanding synthetic test harnesses the engineer can construct, appending an empirical safety margin to the observed maximum latency (the high-water mark). The approach needs no exhaustive microarchitectural model, which explains its ubiquity in complex systems, but it provides no mathematical guarantee against unobserved execution paths or rare microarchitectural collisions. The adversarial stress testing suite developed below seeks to drive the unobserved state space as close to zero as possible.

*Hybrid analysis* measures the execution latency of isolated code snippets or basic blocks directly on physical silicon, then composes those empirical timings across the program's control-flow graph using static path-analysis techniques. It relies on target measurements at the sub-routine scale while adopting the structural path bounds of static modeling.

*Probabilistic analysis* models execution times as random variables, fitting extreme value distributions to empirical latency traces to project the probability that an execution exceeds a given threshold [@cucugrosjean2012measurement]. This methodology assumes that experimental measurement runs faithfully sample the operational probability distribution. On platforms with complex hidden microarchitectural state, unmodeled dependencies can invalidate this assumption; @sec-appendix-systems-timers analyzes these statistical models and their operational limits.

When migrating from an isolated processor to a shared multicore system-on-chip, isolated execution analysis becomes insufficient. Isolated worst-case latency must be augmented with explicit interference penalties for every contended shared resource. Modern multicore response-time frameworks construct these bounds by combining the formal service guarantees of shared arbiters with the maximum request demand generated by co-running cores [@davis2018extensible]. Such composition yields finite, provable bounds only when hardware mechanisms or operating system regulators enforce resource budgets, which is why @sec-placement-isolation-decisions relies on memory-bandwidth regulation (such as MemGuard) to render shared silicon analyzable. Aviation safety standards mandate this exact rigor: FAA AC 20-193 requires system architects to identify every microarchitectural interference channel and establish that unmitigated shared-resource contention is bounded by static analysis and confirmed through worst-case physical testing on the target hardware in its final operational configuration [@faa2024ac20193].

On the running machine, workload placement dictates the verification method. Placing the enforcer on a discrete, dedicated microcontroller makes static timing analysis straightforward and tractable; subsequent hardware testing needs only to evaluate the local real-time threads hosted on that single microcontroller. Conversely, placing the safety monitor on a shared application SoC confines the declared `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.wcet_str` to isolated operation alone. To validate such a shared placement, the engineering team must formally bound $T_{\text{interf,shared}}$ across every shared architectural row identified in @tbl-13-placement-candidates, verify that the resulting response bound remains safely within $T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$, and execute an adversarial campaign capable of refuting both the analytical bounds and the isolation claims.

### Adversarial stress testing and end-to-end brake onset timing

Refuting an independence claim requires synthetic workloads engineered to induce correlated worst-case microarchitectural contention\index{Resource contention!worst-case} rather than standard benchmarks (such as MLPerf) that report average throughput. Standard ML inference pipelines schedule memory transactions to maximize pipeline overlap and average data bus utilization, which conceals transient contention peaks. On physical silicon, maximum interference occurs during synchronized bursts when multiple subsystems demand the exact same physical resources at the exact same clock edge. An adversarial stress suite must synthesize these collision patterns deliberately. The five generators below target the shared die first, because that is where the strongest mechanisms of this chapter live, and they serve two campaigns: refuting a shared-die candidate, or qualifying an island an integrator can use.

1. **Targeted DRAM bank conflict generators**: The stress suite issues unaligned DMA transfers with access strides calibrated to target the exact DRAM bank and bank group assigned to the enforcer's memory buffers. By continuously alternating access across conflicting row addresses, the generator repeatedly evicts open row buffers, incurring the full precharge and activation latency (`{python} PlacementDramTiming.t_conflict_str` ns at the application SoC's memory clock rate) on every subsequent read.
2. **Shared-cache miss-handling engines**: Streaming memory threads cycle through footprints substantially larger than the shared last-level cache. These routines exhaust its MSHRs and saturate writeback buffers with dirty cache lines, triggering the structural interconnect stalls identified in @sec-placement-interference-mechanisms as the primary threat to bounded enforcer latency.
3. **Resonant PDN current-step generators**: Microbenchmarks execute rapid, high-amplitude current transients across neural accelerator arrays while sweeping the transient's phase relative to the permission tick. High-bandwidth oscilloscope probes on the PDN capture package-level $L \cdot dI/dt$ voltage droop and ringing, directly testing whether supply collapse induces clock throttling or logic faults on co-located cores.
4. **Correlated peripheral interrupt storms and storage saturation**: High-bandwidth camera deserializers and NVMe storage controllers stream raw telemetry at line rate while asserting uncoalesced hardware interrupts. This flood stresses the interrupt controller, consumes shared crossbar bandwidth, and saturates system write buffers.
5. **Chassis electromechanical transient coupling**: Test benches inject realistic traction-motor current transients and regenerative braking pulses into the shared DC bus. These tests verify whether DC-DC converter dropout, ground bounce, or electromagnetic interference couples into the enforcer's power rails or clock distribution networks under worst-case operating envelope conditions.

The campaign on the chosen discrete microcontroller keeps only the generators that can reach it, and it maps onto the four fault-injection regimes of @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die, now applied together rather than one at a time. Supply transients on the shared battery bus (generator 5) are regime 1, power-rail droop testing. Clock margining under those transients is regime 2. Saturating the board link while the microcontroller's own receive DMA, fieldbus interrupts, and background plan validation contend for its internal buses (@sec-placement-dispatch-admission) is regime 3, link flooding. Streaming malformed and NaN-laden proposals during all of it is regime 4. Generators 1 to 4 have no target on the microcontroller, which shares no DRAM, cache, or package with the proposer. They drop out because (d) removes those rows, a claim the register readback and the inventory must support, not because the campaign overlooked them.

Hardware instrumentation must trace the complete perception-action timeline: sensor observation capture, coherent ingestion across the interconnect, permission decision completion, drive-frame dispatch over the real-time fieldbus, and physical frame arrival at the motor inverters. While digital bus logs reveal software delays, issuing a bus frame does not equal physical braking. For a controlled powered stop, synchronized motor-phase current probes and external optical tracking must measure the actual onset and dynamic trajectory of vehicle deceleration. The nominal renewal-to-onset budget is `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.renewal_to_onset_str`, combining the software lease duration, one permission tick, fieldbus transit, and motor-drive torque development. Spring-applied mechanical brakes engage only when the vehicle has already decelerated to near-standstill, so mechanical brake contact cannot serve as a proxy for powered deceleration onset. In fault-injection scenarios involving total MCU failure or bus power loss, testing must independently verify the physical stopping distance delivered by the fail-safe emergency circuits. All timing intervals must be reported alongside verified clock synchronization bounds and instrument measurement uncertainties.

Because interference compounds across physical, thermal, and architectural domains, stress testing requires a full factorial experimental matrix to uncover paired-stress vulnerabilities. The evaluation sweeps across four orthogonal axes: a cold condition (an illustrative junction temperature of $35\,^{\circ}\text{C}$) vs. a hot one, which on a shared die means junctions held at or above the throttling threshold $T_{\text{trip}}$ of @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling and on the discrete microcontroller means the bay at its highest qualified ambient; an idle proposal path vs. a saturated proposal engine executing maximum-batch inference; diagnostic circular logging disabled vs. streaming at full non-volatile memory bandwidth; and nominal tracking commands vs. boundary-violating commands that trigger refusal routines. Testing refusal paths under full stress is mandatory because executing a safe clamping trajectory or entering emergency shutdown involves cold branch paths, non-cached error-handling code, and secondary bus transactions that never execute during steady-state aisle driving.

The factorial matrix exists to uncover co-runner collisions that escape isolated unit testing. Consider what happens on the rejected shared-die placement when an unexpected obstacle steps into the warehouse aisle. Detecting the obstacle forces the enforcer to execute its cold refusal branch to initiate an emergency stop. Simultaneously, the application processor flags the anomalous visual scene and triggers a high-priority diagnostic core dump over the shared DMA interconnect. If tested in isolation, the refusal branch executes within its latency budget, and diagnostic dumping runs without error. When triggered concurrently, however, the diagnostic DMA burst floods the shared memory controller precisely when the enforcer must fetch its cold refusal instructions from DRAM. The resulting contention spike stalls the enforcer at the exact moment safe physical actuation is most urgent.

To see how empirical traces refute invalid isolation claims, evaluate an illustrative $10^7$-tick stress test conducted on the rejected shared-die configuration (where the enforcer executes on a real-time core cluster within the application SoC). Operating at one tick per `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.tick_str`, this campaign runs for `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.trace_s_str`, or `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.trace_h_str` h `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.trace_min_str` min `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.trace_sec_str` s of continuous physical execution, excluding platform setup and reset overheads. Under cold, unloaded conditions, enforcer latency remains well within limits: the trace exhibits a median $\text{p50} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.cold_p50_str`, a 99th percentile $\text{p99} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.cold_p99_str`, and a maximum recorded latency of `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.cold_max_str`. Under warm, heavily contended conditions, however, resource conflicts degrade the tail latency: $\text{p50}$ rises to `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.warm_p50_str`, $\text{p99}$ climbs to `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.warm_p99_str`, $\text{p99.9}$ reaches `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.warm_p999_str`, and the observed maximum spikes to `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.warm_max_str`.

Because the loaded $\text{p99}$ alone exceeds the declared isolated bound $T_{\text{wcet}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.wcet_str`, the data immediately refutes the claim that cross-workload interference is negligible ($T_{\text{interf,shared}} = 0$). Once the `{python} PlacementMachine.b_plus_i_str` of local blocking and RTOS task interference is charged, the loaded 99th percentile also pushes the response beyond the enforcer deadline $T_{\text{deadline,enf}} =$ `{python} PlacementSeparationBudget.deadline_str`. A loaded trace of this shape would reach the verdict that the thermal analysis of @sec-placement-thermal-timing-coupling reached from a model, without relying on that model, and the verdict would stand even if the model were wrong. The percentiles here are illustrative; the point is that a real trace on the target, not an argument, is what can refute a placement.

Even if a 10-million-tick stress trace records zero deadline violations, that outcome demonstrates only that interference remained bounded across the specific microarchitectural states generated during the test. A qualification report must document the full latency distribution, observed maximums, total sample counts, and test durations, while explicitly listing all unexercised physical conditions, such as long-term power delivery degradation, transient electromagnetic interference, and silicon aging.[^fn-transistor-aging-guardband]

[^fn-transistor-aging-guardband]: **Transistor Aging (BTI and HCI)**\index{Silicon aging!timing margins}: Bias temperature instability (BTI) and hot-carrier injection (HCI) gradually increase transistor threshold voltages over operational lifetimes. This shift degrades switching speeds across logic gates, an impairment exacerbated during transient voltage droops. Because engineers cannot measure multi-year degradation on fresh silicon, production designs incorporate explicit end-of-life timing guardbands. A physical stress campaign on new development boards cannot certify silicon against aging; the placement qualification record must formally log aging as an analytically budgeted, rather than empirically measured, condition.

When an empirical contention test fails, the engineering team must re-evaluate its architecture: partition memory channels, implement strict arbiter bandwidth caps, restrict proposal workload concurrency, or relocate the enforcer to physically isolated silicon. Conversely, when a campaign passes, it provides empirical evidence that supports the analytical model within the tested parameters, without mistaking a finite empirical sample for an absolute mathematical proof.

::: {#chk-placement-falsification .callout-checkpoint title="Refuting a placement"}

A placement claim is only as strong as the test that could have refuted it. Verify that you can evaluate and defend these empirical criteria:

- [ ] **Threshold arithmetic**: A loaded campaign on a shared-die candidate records one cycle of `{python} PlacementCheckpointEstimates.t_loaded_check_str`. By how much does it exceed the declared `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_str`, how much of the `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` deadline does it leave once blocking and interference are charged, and which claim does it refute?
- [ ] **Isolation and interference**: Can you explain why a loaded cycle below the declared worst-case execution time does not prove that the shared hardware added zero interference?
- [ ] **Method follows placement**: Can you explain why static analysis provides sound bounds for the discrete microcontroller, but fails to yield verifiable bounds on a commercial multicore SoC?
- [ ] **Paired loads**: Can you explain why the enforcer's cold refusal routine must be evaluated concurrently with the application processor's diagnostic memory dump, rather than measured in isolation?

:::

## The Placement Record {#sec-placement-hardware-allocation}

A physical autonomous system cannot rely on informal benchmarks or unwritten assumptions to justify its safety claims. The mobile manipulator now has an assigned hardware placement for its permission path, an explicit deadline, an unloaded execution estimate, and an empirical test suite designed to falsify hardware isolation. However, none of these timing properties can support a release decision unless engineers document them alongside the exact environmental and operational conditions under which they hold.

The **placement record**\index{Placement record!definition}, the eleventh record in the record chain, formalizes where the safety permission path executes and supplies the physical evidence that its timing bounds remain invariant. It consumes the enforcement record of @sec-enforcement-telemetry, inheriting the declared worst-case execution time and hard deadline of the permission path. To these timing constraints it binds the evidence that would show the bound holding under peak proposal load on production silicon: the assigned execution domain, privilege ring, nominal loop period, unloaded and loaded observed maxima, AXI interconnect QoS arbitration settings, PDN inductive droop limits, thermal trip thresholds, enabled hardware mitigations, and a cryptographic digest of the external test ledger (@tbl-13-deployment-envelope-schema). An observed loaded maximum that exceeds the declared worst-case execution time immediately refutes the placement claim. Conversely, observed maxima that fall below the bound validate only the specific conditions exercised during testing; for any empirical latency distribution, sample maxima provide supporting evidence for an upper bound rather than an analytical substitute for it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ That measured maxima support but cannot replace an analytical worst-case bound is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

The placement record bridges architectural configuration registers with direct physical measurements. Register readbacks identify the configured execution enclaves and bus arbitration policies, hardware probes capture voltage rail transients and die temperatures, and cryptographic hashes link high-level summaries directly to fine-grained execution traces:

- `execution_domain_id` and `privilege_and_ring` document the compute domain topology and execution privilege, verified against architectural status registers and the physical system topology.
- `shared_axi_channel_qos` records interconnect arbitration configurations and verifies whether unprivileged software can reconfigure bus priorities; stress tests validate the resulting worst-case latency bounds.
- `max_pdn_droop_thermal_trip` ties voltage supply margins and junction temperature limits to high-bandwidth oscilloscope probe traces and on-die thermal telemetry gathered under full compute load.
- `enforcement_record_digest` and `test_ledger_digest` establish cryptographic provenance, binding the placement record directly to its upstream timing contract and empirical test ledger.

| Field Name                   | Type & Units                                 | Physical System Invariant & Validation Rule                                           | Mobile Manipulator Parameter / Value                                                                             |
|:-----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `execution_domain_id`        | `uint64_t` (enum)                            | Explicit domain topology; confirms physical silicon segregation                       | `0x04` (selected dedicated dual-core lockstep MCU; qualification pending)                                        |
| `privilege_and_ring`         | `uint64_t` (privilege)                       | Record target-specific privilege and memory-protection configuration                  | Proposer: Unprivileged Linux; Enforcer: Bare-Metal MPU                                                           |
| `nominal_period_ns`          | `uint32_t` (ns)                              | Enforcer tick $T_{\text{tick}}$; matches enforcement record `loop_period_ns`          | `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` (`{python} PlacementMachine.tick_ns_str` ns)                                |
| `hard_deadline_ns`           | `uint32_t` (ns)                              | Physical deadline $T_{\text{deadline,enf}}$; matches enforcement record `deadline_ns` | `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` (`{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_ns_str` ns)                        |
| `unloaded_observed_max_ns`   | `uint64_t` (ns)                              | Largest cycle without load; must satisfy $t_{\text{unloaded}} \le T_{\text{wcet}}$    | `0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` (pending; illustrative estimate `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_str` belongs in ledger) |
| `loaded_observed_max_ns`     | `uint64_t` (ns)                              | Peak response under adversarial stress; all ones until qualified                      | `0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` (Awaiting empirical test ledger)                                                            |
| `shared_axi_channel_qos`     | `uint64_t` (QoS mask)                        | Bus QoS configuration plus measured or justified service bound                        | Selected TCM-local bus; topology and access bounds pending verification                                          |
| `max_pdn_droop_thermal_trip` | `uint32_t[2]` (mV; $\text{m}^\circ\text{C}$) | Maximum tolerable rail droop and junction thermal trip threshold                      | Pending target-device characterization; shared-die example values are not MCU limits                             |
| `hardware_mitigation_flags`  | `uint8_t[32]` (bitmask)                      | Qualified hardware isolations only; selections remain in ledger                       | Pending verification; selected rail, TCM, lockstep, and watchdog listed in ledger                                |
| `enforcement_record_digest`  | `uint8_t[32]` (SHA-256)                      | Cryptographic link to upstream enforcement record                                     | SHA-256 digest of @tbl-appendix-systems-wire-enforcement                                                         |
| `test_ledger_digest`         | `uint8_t[32]` (SHA-256)                      | Cryptographic link to full factorial stress campaign ledger                           | Unset until a test ledger exists                                                                                 |

: **Placement record header**: Concrete fields defining the physical compute, memory, thermal, and electrical bounds for deterministic safety enforcement. Loaded observed maximum must remain at or below declared WCET, $T_{\text{wcet}} =$ `{python} PlacementMachine.wcet_str`, under full cognitive stress. {#tbl-13-deployment-envelope-schema tbl-colwidths="[22,18,34,26]"}

The record architecture separates concerns into two distinct structures. A compact, fixed-size header stores critical platform configurations and observed execution maxima for low-overhead verification at boot time. This header anchors an external test ledger via a cryptographic hash. The ledger holds all non-fixed evidentiary records: complete hardware inventories, empirical latency distributions, total sample counts, environmental conditions, active hardware mitigations, and unresolved operational boundaries.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The placement record's field offsets and sizes are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-placement.
:::

For the mobile manipulator, the header records the nominal `{python} PlacementMachine.tick_str` tick period and `{python} PlacementMachine.deadline_str` hard deadline, while the test ledger archives the preliminary `{python} PlacementMachine.unloaded_str` unloaded execution estimate.
